Pick how CLU composes folder cover art. The picker shows a real preview of each style — the previews are generated by running the actual composers, so what you see is what you get.

Style Look Fanned Stack (default) Up to four covers fanned at random rotations. This is the v6.3 look, unchanged. Single Image One cover, full-bleed. Isometric Cascade 3–4 covers with no rotation, stepped 7px up-and-right, with a crisp shadow per layer. 2x2 Mosaic Grid Quad-split into four tiles, 4px interior dividers, one unified outer shadow.

The style is site-wide, not per user — folder art is written to disk as folder.png inside the folder itself, so there is only ever one copy of it to look at.

A folder with fewer than four covers degrades gracefully in every style rather than leaving gaps.

docs.title: Show the folder icon overlay
docs.text: For folders that contain other folders, CLU can draw the composed art inside a folder icon so nested folders read differently from series at a glance. In v6.3 this was hardcoded; it's now its own switch, applied to whichever style you've selected.

docs.title: Regenerate All Thumbnails
docs.text:
Changing the style only affects art generated from that point on. To restyle art you already have, use Regenerate All Thumbnails.

There are two entry points:

From Scope Settings → Personalization Every library. A top-level folder's menu in the collection grid That folder's contents.

It runs on a background thread with live progress in Active Operations, so a large library doesn't hit the gateway timeout the way the old in-request Generate-All-Missing did.

This replaces existing folder art

Regeneration overwrites folder.png for every folder in scope — including art you uploaded by hand. It sits behind a confirmation modal for that reason. Pinned covers survive, because the pin is re-applied when the art is rebuilt.

A sweep never touches the folder you ran it on

Running it on /data/DC Comics restyles every series inside it and leaves that publisher's own folder.png alone. A hand-picked publisher image is not what you're replacing when you restyle your series art. The all-libraries sweep excludes the library roots the same way.

Fixed in v6.4

Single Image could produce a blank thumbnail — it took the first cover blindly, so one corrupt cache entry left an empty folder.png where every other style fell through to the next cover. Unreadable covers are now filtered out before the four-cover cap, so a bad file no longer eats a slot in the other styles either.

folder.webp is now recognized as folder art. Two hardcoded extension lists omitted it, so an uploaded .webp survived a rebuild and kept winning — the new art was generated and then never displayed.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Recommendations stay global

Unlike the theme and dashboard layout, the recommendation service is not a per-user setting. It gates an owner-configured service holding a shared API key, so it is configured once for the whole install rather than per account. See Per-User Data.

This setting let's you configure an AI-powered recommendation service for your reading list. Requires an API key from your preferred provider.

This feature takes your reading history and "Want to Read" list and uses it to generate personalized recommendations for you. Recommendations are manually triggerer, so you can manage how often they run and use them when you want to find something new to read.

docs.title: AI Provider
docs.text:
Select your preferred AI provider from the dropdown. Currently supported providers are:

  • OpenAI (ChatGPT)
  • Anthropic (Claude)
  • Gemini (Google)
  • Local / OpenAI-compatible — Ollama, LM Studio, LocalAI, or any server that speaks the OpenAI API

New in v6.6 — Run recommendations on your own hardware

Choose Local / OpenAI-compatible to keep recommendations entirely on your network. No cloud account is needed.

Selecting it reveals a Base URL field, e.g. http://localhost:11434/v1 for Ollama. If CLU runs in Docker, use http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1. On a Linux host that also needs extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"] in your compose file.

Leave Base URL or Model blank and CLU falls back to the OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_MODEL environment variables.

Local requests time out after 110 seconds. If a large model is slow to answer, try a smaller one.

docs.title: Base URL
docs.text: Shown only for Local / OpenAI-compatible. The address of your local server. It is read only from saved settings, so it can't be changed by a recommendation request.

docs.title: API Key
docs.text: Enter your API key for the selected provider. For Local / OpenAI-compatible the key is optional.

docs.title: Model
docs.text: Enter the model you would like to use for recommendations. As of v6.6 this is a free-text field for every provider, with suggestions for each, so you can type any model you have pulled locally or any newer hosted model.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
The Schedules page is where you configure CLU's recurring background jobs — file-index rebuilds, the GetComics scrape index, Metron series sync, credit backfill, GetComics auto-download, and reading-list sync.

Open it from the gear menu in the top navigation → Schedules.

Times are local, stored as UTC

All schedule times are entered in your local timezone (set on the Personalization page) and stored internally as UTC. If your times look off, check that your timezone is set correctly.

Moved in v6.0

Scheduling used to live on the System & Performance settings tab. In v6.0 it has its own dedicated Schedules page, and a new GetComics Scrape Index schedule was added.

Every schedule works the same way:

Control Description Frequency Disabled, Daily, or Weekly. Disabled turns the job off. Time The time of day (your timezone) to run the job. Day of Week Only shown when frequency is Weekly — which day the job runs. Save Persists that schedule. Each schedule has its own Save button.

docs.title: Index & Sync Management
docs.text: This card manages CLU's SQLite file search index and the jobs that keep your library data current.

docs.title: Index Status
docs.text:
At the top you'll see the current Index Status (file and directory counts), the Last Rebuild time, and the Next Scheduled rebuild. Use Refresh Status to re-check.

Warning

New files won't appear in search or the metadata browser until the index includes them. Either rebuild manually or set an automatic schedule.

docs.title: Rebuild File Index Now
docs.text: Click Rebuild File Index Now to immediately scan your entire data directory and rebuild the index. Use this if search results seem outdated.

docs.title: Automatic Rebuild Schedule
docs.text: Set how often CLU rebuilds the file index automatically (Frequency / Time / Day of Week), then Save Schedule. Default is Disabled.

docs.title: GetComics Scrape Index Schedule
docs.text:
The scrape index pre-populates a local cache of GetComics results — page titles, issue info, and download links — for your tracked series by scraping sitemap URLs. With it populated, wanted-issue searches can answer from the local cache instead of hitting GetComics live every time.

The status area shows how many entries are cached and the next scheduled run. Set the Frequency / Time / Day of Week and click Save Scrape Index Schedule.

New in v6.0

The GetComics scrape index and its schedule are new in v6.0.

docs.title: Automatic Series Sync Schedule
docs.text: Configures how often CLU syncs your tracked series from the Metron API to check for new issues and updated details. Set the schedule and Save Sync Schedule, or click Sync Now to run it immediately. The last sync and next run are shown below the buttons.

docs.title: Credit Backfill
docs.text:
New in v6.4

CLU can find comics that were tagged without creator credits and repair them automatically.

docs.title: Why your comics have no credits
docs.text:
Comics tagged on release morning frequently came out with no creator credits at all. Two files from the same sweep, five seconds apart, would come out one with full credits and one with none — both naming Metron as the source, and Metron's API holding full credits for both.

Two causes compound:

  1. The Metron client library's response cache had no working TTL. It never checked the expiry column, and its cleanup only ran at startup — so on a long-lived container the effective TTL was process uptime. A fresh fetch could never displace a stale row; the old one had to be deleted outright.
  2. Metron finishes issue records after a comic ships. One reported issue was still being edited on Metron two hours after the file was written.

Either way the file was stuck permanently: once ComicInfo.xml carries a Notes field, every automatic tagging path skips that file forever — and a manual re-tag was a no-op, because the cache purge only dropped series responses and never the issue detail, which is the response carrying the credits. That's fixed too: Refresh from Metron on a series page now drops the issue bodies as well, and bulk re-tag with overwrite existing fetches through the purging path rather than rewriting the same half-entered record it was meant to repair.

docs.title: How the sweep works
docs.text:
The backfill runs in two passes against one shared fetch budget:

Pass What it does Changed records Asks Metron which issues have been modified since the last sweep — the field that moves when an editor finishes a half-entered record — joins that list against your library, and repairs those. One paged call replaces a detail fetch per candidate, and it finds a comic tagged a year ago whose record was completed last night. Credit-less files The safety net for the other cause. When a file was tagged from a stale cached body, Metron's record may never have changed, so the first pass never mentions it. Recently written credit-less files are re-fetched directly.

Two guarantees worth knowing:

  • A file is only rewritten when Metron now actually has credits. A run that finds nothing touches no bytes.
  • The rewrite merges. Tags the file already carries — your Genre, your own edits — survive.

Candidates are limited to a 45-day window on the file's modification time, so a comic Metron will never have credits for ages out of scope instead of being re-fetched every night forever. The fetch budget caps Metron requests, not files examined — skips are nearly free — and a run stops early on either the budget or a spent daily quota.

No rescan, no restart

The join uses a new indexed column holding each file's Metron issue id. Existing rows are filled in by the metadata scanner in the background, at the lowest priority, whenever it has nothing else pending. There is no big-bang rescan to trigger and nothing to wait for on upgrade.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Control What it does Enable credit backfill Runs the sweep automatically after each series sync. Backfill Credits Now Runs it immediately, on demand.

The on-demand run is backgrounded with progress in Active Operations, since a full sweep is paced at roughly 15 requests a minute and would outlast the gateway timeout.

The automatic run sits behind its own guard, so a backfill problem can never fail the series sync.

Metron only, for now

ComicVine has the same shape of problem — a day-of-release ComicVine issue often has no credits, and the same "already has Notes" skip locks it in. The candidate query is provider-agnostic, so a ComicVine arm can be added later.

docs.title: GetComics Auto-Download Schedule
docs.text:
Configures how often CLU searches GetComics for wanted issues (with today's release date or later) and queues downloads. Set the schedule and Save GetComics Schedule, or click Download Now to run it immediately.

Weekly Packs takes over

If Weekly Packs is enabled, individual-issue auto-download is disabled and this section is greyed out — a banner links you to Manage Weekly Packs. Disable Weekly Packs to re-enable per-issue auto-download here.

Downloaded files are moved to the Series Folder once processed, and metadata is added at that time if missing.

New in v6.5 — one sweep at a time, and a ceiling on it

If a scheduled run is already in progress, Download Now and the next scheduled trigger stand down rather than starting a second copy that re-queues everything the first run is still working through.

A single sweep also queues at most 150 downloads. That's a blast-radius limit, not a throughput limit — hitting it stops that run and the rest is picked up on the next one. See Downloading the right comic.

Progress now reports into Active Operations, so a multi-hour run is visible from anywhere in the app.

docs.title: Reading List Sync Schedule
docs.text:
Automatically syncs your reading lists so CLU can pick up upstream changes without you visiting each list. Set the Frequency / Time / Day of Week and click Save Reading List Sync Schedule.

Updated in v6.5 — it's no longer GitHub-only

This job used to sync GitHub-sourced lists only. As of v6.5 it syncs every list that has a syncable source: GitHub CBL URLs, Metron reading lists, Metron story arcs and ComicVine story arcs.

Lists you built by hand, or imported from an uploaded .cbl file, have no remote copy to compare against and are skipped.

Each run asks the cheap question first and only rebuilds a list when the source has actually changed, so a nightly schedule on an unchanged library is close to free.

Metron lists are pre-filtered in one call

A library with dozens of imported Metron lists would otherwise cost dozens of requests per run. CLU asks Metron once which of your lists have moved, then only re-reads those — so the schedule scales with how much changed, not with how many lists you have.

Story arcs are checked differently, because an arc's own last-modified date never moves when an issue is added to it. See Why an arc syncs differently from a reading list.

docs.title: System and Performance Settings
docs.text:
Settings related to system performance and operations are managed on the System and Performance tab.

Scheduling moved to its own page

Index rebuilds, Metron sync, GetComics auto-download, and the other recurring jobs are no longer configured here — they're on the dedicated Schedules page (also in the gear menu).

docs.title: Performance & Timeout Settings
docs.text:
These help you manage large files depending on your system. The default settings on an average system will easily handle converting a 2GB CBR to CBZ.

Setting Description Operation Timeout (seconds) Timeout for large file operations (convert, rebuild). Default 3600 (1 hour). Minimum 300 (5 minutes), maximum 7200. Large File Threshold (MB) Files larger than this get enhanced progress reporting. Default 500 MB (range 100–2000).

docs.title: Timezone Settings
docs.text: Set your local Timezone so reading history and other date/time information — including Schedules times and the Insights page — display and run correctly for you.

docs.title: Cache Management
docs.text: Click Clear All Caches to clear the directory cache and the statistics cache (Insights charts). Use this if data appears stale after moving or editing files.

docs.title: Missing Issue Configuration
docs.text:
These two settings tune the Missing Issue Check. How much they matter depends on how heavily you use that feature and how your library is structured.

Setting Description IGNORED TERMS Comma-separated words/terms to ignore while scanning for missing issues. Update these and re-run the check to better parse your library. IGNORED FILES Comma-separated file names to ignore when checking for missing issues (e.g. cover.jpg, cvinfo).

docs.title: Logging & Debugging
docs.text:
Enable Debug Logging adds detailed diagnostic messages to the App Logs. This helps with troubleshooting but increases log file size. Changes take effect after saving. See Debug Logging for what the output looks like.

Tip

When reporting a problem, enable debug logging, reproduce the issue, then use Download Debug Package on the Logs page to bundle everything up (with secrets redacted).

docs.title: ComicInfo.XML Update Settings
docs.text:
These features update/clean the ComicInfo.xml inside archives. The process runs on a single directory: it extracts the ComicInfo.xml, makes the updates below, and recompresses the file. Consider them experimental — they've been tested the least.

Update Volume to First Issue Year: When there's no volume year in the ComicInfo.xml, this reads the 4-digit year from the alphanumerically-first file in the folder and applies it as the volume year for each file.

Remove ALL Markdown Content from Comments: Removes headers, bold text, and tables from the Comments field of the ComicInfo.xml.

Remove 'Covers & Creators' Table: Removes a Covers & Creators table from the Comments field of the ComicInfo.xml.

docs.title: Save & Restart
docs.text:
Save System & Performance Settings: Saves any changes made on this tab.

Restart App: Only needed on the initial install and as a quick way to force a restart to reload config/settings changes. The Restart App button lives at the bottom of the Personalization tab.

docs.title: Collection Homepage
docs.text:
Example Collection Landing Page with Favorites and Reading Lists Example Collection Publisher Page with Nested Folders

CLU provides a visual browser to navigate your collection. Generally this is grouped by publisher, but CLU will render any folder structure you have.

docs.title: Viewing Multiple Libraries
docs.text: If you have multiple libraries, you can select which library you want to view from the dropdown menu in the top left of the collection page.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Currently, there are up to 6 sections that can show on the collection page:

Dashboard Customization

The order of these sections and which ones are hidden is a per-user setting. Arrange your dashboard from My Account; administrators can set the site default for new accounts.

docs.title: Publisher
docs.text:
This is the default section. It displays all publishers in your collection and is always available. Clicking into a publisher displays all series folders or issues within that publisher.

Note

In documentation, this is referred to as the "Publisher" section, but it reflects whatever folder structure you have in your collection.

With multiple libraries configured, this section updates dynamically based on your selected library. Your Per page choice when browsing is saved and restored across navigation.

docs.title: Favorite Collections
docs.text: Displays all publishers that have been marked as a favorite. You can favorite a publisher by clicking the icon in the top left of the publisher list.

docs.title: Want to Read List
docs.text:
This section draws from two sources:

  • Flagged files and folders: Mark a series folder or issue as "Want to Read" by clicking the icon in the top left of the list, or via the Want to Read action in the folder dropdown (see Additional Features).
  • Bookmarked reading lists: Each bookmarked list appears as a single card featuring a cover stack, read/total progress count, and a direct link to the list.

docs.title: Continue Reading
docs.text: Displays issues that have been started but not completed. Clicking the icon removes an issue from this section.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text: Generates personalized recommendations based on your reading history and Want to Read list. Recommendations are manually triggered so you can run them on demand when looking for something new. You must configure an API key in Recommendations to enable this feature.

docs.title: On the Stack
docs.text:
The On the Stack section alerts you to new issues for series that you are currently reading, ensuring you stay caught up.

For example, if you have read Absolute Batman 001 through Absolute Batman 017, issue 018 will appear on the stack as soon as it is added to your library.

Note

Only the next unread issue in sequence is shown. If both Absolute Batman 018 and Absolute Batman 019 are unread, only issue 018 is displayed until it is marked as read.

On the Stack draws from two sources:

  • Series in your Pull List: If you want to exclude certain series, toggle the stack option on the Series page.
  • Bookmarked reading lists: Each bookmarked list contributes its next unread issue, displayed with a list-name badge.

If a bookmarked list and a subscribed series point to the same next issue, it is deduplicated and shown once.

docs.title: Recently Added
docs.text: Displays the last 100 issues added to your collection.

docs.title: All Books
docs.text: By default, All Books sorts by series, then parent folder, then issue number (with cover year used as a tiebreaker). This keeps different volumes of the same series grouped together. Volumes kept loose in the same folder sort by issue number within that folder.

docs.title: The Pager
docs.text:
The pagination control is sticky, pinning to the bottom of the viewport while browsing and settling inline at the true bottom of the page.

The pager pinned to the bottom of the viewport over a full grid.

The pager includes:

  • Windowed page numbers with ellipsis navigation for large libraries.
  • A "Showing X–Y of Z" readout.
  • A mirrored Per page selector so you can adjust page size without scrolling back to the top.
  • Seamless compatibility with Multi-Select mode so bulk action controls do not obstruct pagination.

docs.title: Card Size
docs.text:
Toggle between Standard and Large card sizes in the filter bar.

Like Per page, this setting is saved in your browser rather than your account, allowing device-specific preferences (e.g. standard on desktop, large on tablet).

docs.title: Folder Art
docs.text:
Folder cover art is generated automatically as you browse. When the grid encounters a folder without cached art, it queues a background task to generate it.

Folder art generation behavior:

Behavior Detail Serialized processing Archive extraction is processed one folder at a time to preserve system resources. Request deduplication A folder is never queued more than once concurrently. Backoff on error Folders that fail thumbnail generation are paused for 6 hours before retrying. Preserves existing art Uploaded or pre-existing art is never overwritten by automatic generation.

CLU recognizes folder.png, folder.jpg, folder.jpeg, folder.gif, and folder.webp as folder art.

Generated folder art supports four styles — Fanned Stack (default), Single Image, Isometric Cascade, and 2x2 Mosaic Grid — selectable site-wide on the Personalization page. You can pin a specific issue's cover as a folder's primary art with Set as Folder Thumbnail, or restyle all existing folders with Regenerate All Thumbnails.

Automatic folder art generation can be disabled in File Processing Settings.

docs.title: Comic Covers
docs.text:
Comic covers update automatically whenever an issue is edited, rebuilt, or retagged. The grid also detects when a comic archive is newer than its cached thumbnail and updates accordingly.

  • Non-image formats: Files without cover extractors (such as standalone PDFs) and macOS system sidecars (._*) are automatically skipped during generation and are not flagged as errors.
  • Corrupted archives: If cover extraction fails due to a damaged archive, the file is logged to the Problem Files page under Thumbnail with the exact error, where you can retry extraction or find a replacement.

docs.title: Access in a Multi-User Install
docs.text:
In a multi-user install:

  • Readers see a clean browsing grid without action menus, Multi-Select, or bulk action bars (which are reserved for Clerk and Admin roles).
  • Content visibility is governed by library and folder grants. Recently Added is automatically filtered to include only folders the current user has permission to view.

docs.title: Collection Browsing (Issues)
docs.text:
Example Issues Page

When you open a series folder, CLU displays a grid of all comic issues in that folder.

The issue number is displayed in the top right corner of each cover for quick identification.

Issue Number

docs.title: Issue Options
docs.text:
Click the menu on any issue card to access file actions:

Example Issue Dropdown Menu

  1. Crop Cover: Crops the first image of the CBZ, saving the right half as the new cover and the full spread as the second page. See Crop Cover.
  2. Remove First Image: Removes the first image from the issue. It is recommended to check the issue in Edit File first to confirm the target image is truly page one. See Remove First Image.
  3. Edit File: Unpacks the CBZ archive to let you reorder, remove, or edit pages and metadata. See Edit File.
  4. Rebuild: Rebuilds an incorrectly structured CBZ archive or converts a CBR file into a clean CBZ. See Rebuild.
  5. Enhance: Enhances image quality across all pages in the issue. See Enhance.
  6. Set as Folder Thumbnail: Pins this issue's cover as the primary art for the folder. See Set as Folder Thumbnail below.
  7. Delete: Deletes the issue file from disk. See Delete.

docs.title: Set as Folder Thumbnail
docs.text:
You can pin any comic issue's cover as the parent folder's cover art.

Click the menu on the issue whose cover you want to use and select Set as Folder Thumbnail. The folder's art is regenerated immediately with that issue featured as its primary cover.

"Primary" adapts automatically to each folder art style:

Style Where the pinned cover appears Single Image Displays as the entire cover image. Fanned Stack Positioned as the front card of the stack. Isometric Cascade Positioned as the front card of the cascade. 2x2 Mosaic Grid Positioned as the top-left tile.

Pinned covers are stored per folder and persist through bulk restyling, so running Regenerate All Thumbnails applies the new style without losing your selection.

Comics only

Only comic archive files can be pinned as folder thumbnails. Pinned text or auxiliary image files cannot be used.

Changing or removing a pinned thumbnail

To change the pinned cover, select Set as Folder Thumbnail on another issue. To use a custom image instead, place a folder.png, folder.jpg, or folder.webp file in the folder — custom uploaded art always takes precedence over generated thumbnails.

docs.title: Collection Browsing (Publishers)
docs.text:
Example Publisher Page with Custom Header

CLU allows you to visually browse your collection starting from your root library (/data) directory. While this documentation refers to top-level directories as "Publishers", they represent whatever folder structure exists in your storage.

Each folder includes a menu providing folder-level management actions.

docs.title: Publisher Folders
docs.text:
The folder menu provides three options:

  • Scan Files: Scans the directory and updates the database for this publisher, indexing newly added files and structural changes.
  • Generate Missing Thumbnails: Generates cover thumbnails for all folders that are currently missing art. See Generating Thumbnails.
  • Missing File Check: Analyzes the folder to detect missing issues in series sequences. See Missing File Check.

docs.title: Custom Headers
docs.text: Folders support custom banner headers. CLU checks for an image file named header.png, header.jpg, or header.gif in the publisher folder. If present, it is rendered across the top of the page. The recommended image resolution is 2200×516 pixels.

docs.title: Custom Thumbnails
docs.text: All folders support custom thumbnails. Place an image named folder.png, folder.jpg, folder.jpeg, folder.gif, or folder.webp in the directory, and CLU will use it as the folder's cover image. Recommended dimensions are 200×300 pixels.

docs.title: Uploading a Publisher Thumbnail
docs.text:
You can quickly assign a custom thumbnail by dragging and dropping an image file directly onto the publisher card from your computer.

Uploading a Thumbnail via Drag and Drop

Once uploaded, the new cover art displays automatically on the publisher card.

docs.title: Favorite Publisher
docs.text: Click the icon in the top left of any publisher card to mark it as a favorite. This pins the publisher to the Favorite Collections row on your dashboard for fast access.

docs.title: Navigating to Series
docs.text: Clicking any publisher card opens that publisher's page, displaying all child series folders or standalone comic issues within it.

docs.title: Reading Lists
docs.text:
CLU supports importing curated reading lists and publisher story arcs from multiple sources, as well as creating, organizing, and sharing your own custom lists.

Reading Lists Page

docs.title: Importing Reading Lists
docs.text:
You can import reading lists from several sources:

  • DieselTech GitHub Repository — Browse and import from a curated repository of ComicBookLover (.cbl) reading lists.
  • Import by URL — Paste a direct URL pointing to a .cbl file on GitHub or the web.
  • Upload CBL File — Upload a local .cbl or .xml file from your device.
  • Metron Reading Lists — Search and import curated reading lists from the Metron comic database.
  • Metron Story Arcs — Import publisher story arcs from Metron as ordered reading lists.
  • ComicVine Story Arcs — Import major events and story arcs from ComicVine.

docs.title: GitHub Repository Browser
docs.text:
GitHub Import Modal

Click GitHub Import to open the browser modal. The Browse Repository tab indexes reading lists from the DieselTech/CBL-ReadingLists repository:

  1. Use the search input to filter lists by title or character.
  2. Select files using the checkboxes, or choose Select All / Deselect All.
  3. Click Import Selected to initiate a batch import.

Selected lists are downloaded and processed in the background. Up to 5 imports process concurrently, with the remainder queued and visible in the progress tracker.

docs.title: Import by URL
docs.text: Select the Import by URL tab to paste a direct link to any .cbl file on GitHub. CLU automatically converts standard GitHub blob links to raw content download URLs.

docs.title: Upload CBL File
docs.text: Click Upload CBL to upload a .cbl or .xml file directly from your local machine. The list is parsed and added immediately.

docs.title: Metron Import
docs.text:
Metron Import Modal

Click Metron Import to open the Metron browser. Two options are available:

  • Reading Lists — Search and browse Metron's curated reading lists. Issue reading orders and descriptions are preserved.
  • Story Arcs — Browse publisher story arcs with infinite scroll pagination. Issues are ordered according to their chronological arc sequence.

Note: Metron credentials must be configured in Settings > Metadata Providers prior to importing.

docs.title: ComicVine Import
docs.text:
ComicVine Import Modal

Click ComicVine Import to search and import crossover story arcs and events from ComicVine. A ComicVine API key must be configured in Settings > Metadata Providers.

docs.title: Provider Import Features
docs.text:
When browsing Metron or ComicVine imports, the modal provides:

  • Search filter — Live filter results by name as you type.
  • Bulk selection — Use Select All and Deselect All to import multiple arcs at once.
  • Selection counter — Displays the total count of selected items.
  • Infinite scroll — Automatically loads additional arc pages while scrolling.

docs.title: Filtering and Searching Lists
docs.text: On the main Reading Lists page, a tag filter bar appears whenever lists have tags assigned. Click a tag to isolate lists with that tag, or select All to view every list.

docs.title: Import Status
docs.text: During active imports, the header displays a live progress status bar showing current issue matching, completed items, and remaining items in the queue.

docs.title: Keeping an Imported List Up to Date
Sync
docs.text:
The Sync button re-reads the original remote source and updates your reading list to reflect newly published or updated reading orders:

Source Sync Action Change Detection GitHub CBL URL Re-downloads the remote .cbl file File contents check Metron reading list Re-reads the list from Metron Last-modified timestamp Metron story arc Re-checks issue members of the arc Arc membership diff ComicVine story arc Re-checks issue members of the arc Arc membership diff

If no upstream changes have occurred, Sync finishes immediately. When changes are found, the reading list rebuilds asynchronously in the background.

Sync Availability

Custom lists created by hand or imported via local file upload do not have an upstream URL and do not display a Sync button. To update a list you already own, use Sync rather than re-importing, which would produce a duplicate list.

docs.title: Sync vs. Re-match
docs.text:
The Sync and Re-match buttons serve distinct purposes:

Button Target Purpose Sync Remote Source Re-reads the upstream provider (GitHub, Metron, ComicVine) and adjusts list contents to match. Re-match Local Library Re-scans your local files to match open entries against newly acquired or renamed files.

Use Sync when the upstream reading list has been modified. Use Re-match when files in your library have been added, renamed, or converted.

docs.title: Scheduled Syncing
docs.text: Automated recurring sync can be configured in Reading List Sync Schedule to keep all remote lists updated automatically.

docs.title: Track Wanted
docs.text:
Click the Track Wanted toggle on any reading list to monitor missing issues:

  • Any entry on the list without a matching local file is flagged as a wanted issue.
  • Missing entries appear on the Wanted page under the From Reading Lists tab and are searched during automated nightly downloader runs (GetComics, Usenet, DC++).
  • Entries lacking a series title or issue number are ignored.

Opt-In Per List

Track Wanted is disabled by default on newly imported lists to prevent automatic search sweeps for hundreds of issues until you choose to track that specific list.

docs.title: Nothing is stored, so nothing goes stale
docs.text: "Unmatched" is the definition of a tracked wanted issue — no separate secondary tracking list is maintained. Mapping an entry to a local file by hand removes it from the Wanted section immediately, and clearing the mapping brings it back.

docs.title: Creating a Reading List
docs.text: Click Create List on the Reading Lists page, enter a title for the new list, and click Create. You can immediately begin adding comic issues.

docs.title: Adding Issues to a Reading List
docs.text: Issues can be added through two workflows:

docs.title: Add via Search
docs.text:
Click Add Issue inside any reading list to open the search modal:

  1. Search by title, series, or keyword across your CLU file index.
  2. Select the desired issue from the results list.
  3. Click Add to List.

docs.title: Add via Collection Browser
docs.text: From any issue card in the collection browser or Source Wall, open the menu and select Add to List. A modal will prompt you to select which reading list to add the issue to.

docs.title: Adjusting Reading Order
docs.text:
Click Reorder in the reading list detail view to enter ordering mode:

  1. The grid switches to a drag-and-drop layout.
  2. Drag and reposition issue cards into your desired reading sequence.
  3. Click Save Order to persist the new sequence.

docs.title: Mapping Missing Issues
docs.text:
For imported lists where an entry did not automatically find a matching local file, click the placeholder cover card or select Map Issue from the three-dot menu to link a file.

Mapping an unmatched issue to a local comic file

You can also search for and trigger a download for missing issues directly from the mapping dialog.

Searching for a missing issue across download sources

docs.title: Automatic Match Persistence
docs.text:
CLU automatically preserves reading list associations:

  • Follows file moves and conversions: Renaming a file, moving it to another directory, or converting from CBR to CBZ preserves all reading list mappings.
  • Immediate gap filling: When a new comic download arrives in your library, CLU immediately evaluates open entries on tracked reading lists and maps matching files without waiting for a re-scan.
  • Volume and year precision: Matcher logic takes publication year and volume numbering into account to ensure different series with identical issue numbering are not confused.

docs.title: Managing Tags
docs.text:
Click the Tags button on any reading list card to manage its tags:

  • Type to create new tags with autocomplete suggestions from existing tags.
  • Click tag badges to quickly toggle them.
  • Use assigned tags to filter lists on the main Reading Lists index.

docs.title: Bookmarking a List
docs.text: Click the Bookmark button on any reading list card to add it to your personal dashboard. Bookmarks are personal to each user account and do not affect other users in multi-user installs.

docs.title: Want to Read
docs.text:
A bookmarked reading list displayed as a Want to Read card

Bookmarked lists appear as a card in the Want to Read row on your collection homepage, providing:

  • A layered cover stack drawn from the list's issues.
  • A read / total count badge.
  • A visual progress bar indicating completion.
  • Direct click-through access to the reading list.

docs.title: On the Stack
docs.text:
Bookmarked lists feed your On the Stack dashboard section with their next unread issue:

  • An issue is eligible for the stack if it is the first unread entry in reading order that has a matched local file.
  • Unmatched missing entries are skipped, allowing you to advance through available issues.
  • Each issue displays a badge indicating the source reading list.
  • If a bookmarked list and an active Pull List series point to the same comic, it is deduplicated and shown once.

docs.title: Searching for Missing Issues
docs.text: Clicking a missing issue in a reading list opens the multi-source search modal, allowing you to locate and queue downloads across GetComics, Usenet, and DC++, ranked according to your configured Source Priority. Search queries automatically incorporate the release year for precise results.

docs.title: Reading Lists and Roles
docs.text:
In a multi-user install:

  • Readers can browse shared reading lists, read issues, and manage their own dashboard bookmarks.
  • Creating, importing, editing, deleting, mapping, reordering, syncing, and toggling Track Wanted are restricted to Clerk and Administrator roles.

docs.title: Reading Comics
docs.text:
Reading a Comic

When browsing your collection, click on any comic card to open it in the built-in reader modal.

docs.title: Read vs. Unread Status
docs.text:
Read vs. Unread Status

When reading a comic, it is automatically marked as completed and added to your reading history once you pass 90% of the pages.

Completed and in-progress comics display a reading status icon in the corner of the cover badge next to the issue number.

docs.title: Reader Features
docs.text:
The reader is designed for lightweight, high-performance reading across desktop and mobile devices:

  1. Instant Loading: Pages load on demand, pre-buffering upcoming pages in the background as you read.
  2. Responsive Layout: Adapts automatically across desktop monitors, tablets, and mobile phones.
  3. Page Counter: Displays the current page number alongside the total page count.
  4. Progress Bar: Shows visual progress through the issue. Reaching 90% automatically marks the issue as read.
  5. Direct Navigation: Use the scrubber dots along the bottom or the page selector to jump directly to any page.
  6. Toggleable Controls: The header and footer overlay the top and bottom of the page. Tap or click anywhere on the page to toggle controls on or off. Double-click or double-tap to zoom.

docs.title: Resuming Reading
docs.text:
Resume Reading

If you close the reader before reaching the 90% completion threshold, CLU saves your position. The next time you open the issue, a prompt offers to resume reading from that exact page or start over from page one.

You can also manually set a bookmark at any time by clicking the icon in the reader header.

docs.title: Reading Position & History Persistence
docs.text:
Reading progress and bookmarks follow robust persistence rules:

  • Follows file operations: If you rename an issue, move it to a different directory, or convert it from CBR to CBZ, your reading progress and bookmarks remain intact.
  • Autosave on exit: Reading positions save automatically when closing the reader, switching tabs, or refreshing the browser, preventing lost progress on mobile devices.
  • Per-user privacy: In multi-user setups, reading progress, history, and bookmarks are isolated to each user account.

docs.title: Collection Browsing (Series)
docs.text:
Example Collection Series Page

Opening a publisher displays all child series folders and standalone issues contained in that directory.

docs.title: Series Options
docs.text:
For any series folder, clicking the menu provides management options:

Example Series Dropdown Menu

  1. Generate Thumbnail: Generates a thumbnail for the folder based on its contents if art is missing.
  2. Missing File Check: Checks for missing issues within the series based on the Missing File Check.
  3. Delete: Deletes the folder and all contained files after confirmation.

docs.title: Generating Thumbnails
docs.text:
Example of Generating Thumbnails

To generate a thumbnail for a series, select Generate Thumbnail from the folder menu. CLU builds an image from the folder's contents:

  1. Single-issue folders: Uses the cover of that issue as the folder thumbnail.
  2. Multi-issue folders: Composes art using up to the first four issues according to your selected folder art style. In the default Fanned Stack style, the first issue forms the front cover with subtle offset rotation.
  3. Nested folders: Uses the lead cover from up to four child folders, with an optional folder glyph overlay (see folder icon overlay).

CLU supports four thumbnail layout styles: Fanned Stack, Single Image, Isometric Cascade, and 2x2 Mosaic Grid. These can be chosen site-wide under Personalization. You can also pin an exact issue cover as the front image using Set as Folder Thumbnail.

docs.title: Regenerate All Thumbnails
docs.text:
Changing the folder art style in settings applies to newly generated art going forward. To restyle folders you already have, use Regenerate All Thumbnails.

On any top-level publisher folder, select Regenerate All Thumbnails from the menu to update every series folder within it. A global version covering all libraries is available on the Personalization page.

Regeneration runs asynchronously in the background with live progress displayed in Active Operations.

Preserves publisher art and pinned covers

Running this operation on a publisher restyles child series art while leaving that publisher's own custom header and cover art untouched. Any series with a pinned issue cover will preserve that chosen cover within the updated layout.

docs.title: Mark a Series as "Want to Read"
docs.text: Click the icon in the top left of the series list to add it to your Want to Read list. This surfaces the series in the Want to Read row on your collection homepage and in your OPDS feed.

docs.title: Source Wall
docs.text:
Example Source Wall

The Source Wall provides a tabular, spreadsheet-style view of your library with detailed metadata columns. It is designed for auditing tags, inspecting file properties, and executing file actions across your collection.

Source Wall Publishers View

docs.title: Column Configuration
docs.text:
You can customize visible columns by clicking the icon in the top right corner of the Source Wall view.

Config Options

Use the column selector to toggle which metadata fields and technical properties appear in the table.

docs.title: Issue Actions
docs.text:
You can open and read any issue directly by clicking the icon in its row.

Click the menu on any row to access issue operations:

Example Issue Dropdown Menu

  1. Crop Cover: Crops the first image of the CBZ, saving the right side as the new cover and the full spread as the second image. See Crop Cover.
  2. Remove First Image: Removes the first image from the issue. See Remove First Image.
  3. Edit Pages: Unpacks the CBZ to edit or reorder pages and metadata. See Edit File.
  4. Rebuild: Rebuilds an improperly constructed CBZ file or converts a CBR to CBZ format. See Rebuild.
  5. Enhance: Enhances image quality across all pages in the comic. See Enhance.
  6. Add Blank to End: Appends a blank .png file named zzzz9999 to the end of the archive to fix two-page spread alignment in manga readers.
  7. Fetch Metadata: Queries metadata providers to retrieve comic information and generate a ComicInfo.xml file. See Get ComicInfo.xml.
  8. Info: Displays technical metadata and the full contents of ComicInfo.xml (e.g., page count, resolution, archive details).
  9. Delete: Deletes the issue from your library. See Delete.

docs.title: DC++ Downloads
docs.text:
New in v6.3

DC++ support is new in v6.3. It is a third download source alongside File Downloads (GetComics) and Usenet — not a replacement for either.

CLU can search DC++ hubs and queue downloads from them. Completed bundles land in your WATCH folder through the same mover Usenet uses, so import behaves identically to every other source once the file arrives.

docs.title: The target is AirDC++, not DC++
docs.text:
You need the AirDC++ Web Client

CLU talks to the AirDC++ Web Client through its REST API. It does not talk to DC++ itself, or to ApexDC, FlylinkDC, or any other DC++ client.

Those clients have no remote API for CLU to call. Pointing CLU at one will not work, and no amount of host/port fiddling will change that.

AirDC++ Web Client is a separate application that you install and run yourself. It connects to your hubs, and CLU drives it — much the same relationship CLU has with SABnzbd or NZBGet on the Usenet side.

docs.title: How it fits the pipeline
docs.text:
Step What happens 1. Search CLU asks your AirDC++ instance to search its connected hubs, then scores the results the same way it scores GetComics and Usenet results. 2. Grab You pick a result (or auto-download picks one). CLU queues it in AirDC++ and records the job in its database. 3. Download AirDC++ downloads the bundle from the hub. CLU polls it for progress and shows it on the Download Status page. 4. Import When the bundle completes, CLU moves it into WATCH, where folder monitoring picks it up exactly as it would a Usenet or direct download.

Because step 4 is shared, everything downstream — renaming, metadata, filing into the library — is identical no matter which source the file came from.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A running AirDC++ Web Client instance, reachable from CLU over HTTP.
  • An AirDC++ username and password with API access.
  • At least one hub connected in AirDC++, sharing comics.
  • A download folder that AirDC++ writes to and CLU can also read. See the two-paths warning — this is the single most common setup mistake.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Adding AirDC++ — connecting CLU to your instance, and getting the two path settings right.
  • Searching & Grabbing — the DC++ section of the search modal, scoring, and why hub searches take ~30 seconds.
  • Status & Restart Recovery — tracking bundles, and what survives a container restart.

DC++ also participates in Source Priority, which now ranks three sources rather than two.

docs.title: Searching & Grabbing
docs.text: Once AirDC++ is configured, DC++ appears as a third section in CLU's source-search modal, alongside GetComics and Usenet.

docs.title: Where you can search
docs.text:
• Series page (manual search) — searching for a specific issue queries GetComics, your Usenet indexers, and your DC++ hubs.
  • Wanted Issues — the same combined search runs from your wanted list.
  • Reading Lists — the reading-list search modal gained Usenet and DC++ sections in v6.3; it was GetComics-only before.

Each source gets its own labeled section header, ordered by Source Priority.

The modal searches everything you've configured

Source Priority controls the order of these sections, and it governs which sources the auto-download cascade uses. The manual modal queries every configured source regardless of ranking — a client you never ranked is still searchable by hand. See Source Priority.

docs.title: Hub searches are slow — that's normal
docs.text:
Hub searches are slow

A DC++ search typically takes around 30 seconds. This is not CLU stalling.

AirDC++ queues searches and paces them per hub to avoid getting you kicked. Measured against a live two-hub setup, the query wasn't even dispatched for roughly 17 seconds, with results settling around 30 seconds.

CLU waits on the AirDC++ instance's own progress counters rather than a fixed timeout — an earlier flat timeout gave up before the query had even been sent. The wait is capped at 45 seconds, and CLU returns early once results stop arriving.

Usenet and GetComics results appear far faster. Expect the DC++ section to fill in last.

docs.title: Result scoring
docs.text:
DC++ results run through the same scorer as GetComics and Usenet, and collapse into the same three tiers:

Tier Meaning ACCEPT A confident match for the series, issue, and year. Eligible for auto-download. FALLBACK A plausible match with something missing or ambiguous. Used only when nothing better exists. REJECT Not a match. Shown for manual review, never auto-grabbed.

Alongside the tier, results show the number of users sharing the file — a higher count generally means a faster, more reliable download.

docs.title: Back-catalogue naming
docs.text:
Comic hubs name older files in their own dialect:

196103 Strange Tales v1 083.cbz

That's a YYYYMM cover-date prefix and a vN volume token — a shape the shared scorer, which expects scene-style Series 083 (1961), does not recognize. Every date-prefixed file previously scored REJECT, which made the entire Golden and Silver Age catalogue unreachable while modern releases matched fine.

CLU now normalizes these titles before scoring, so the back catalogue is matchable.

Two details worth knowing:

  • Displayed titles are the real filename. Only the scored form is normalized. What you see in the results list is exactly what's on the hub, so you can always tell what you're grabbing.
  • The declared volume is compared separately. Stripping the vN token to make the title scorable would also throw away the scorer's chance to catch a volume mismatch, so CLU extracts the volume first and rejects a wrong one on its own.

docs.title: Grabbing a result
docs.text:
Click download on any DC++ result and CLU queues the bundle in AirDC++, then tracks it on the Download Status page. When it completes, CLU moves it into WATCH and the normal import pipeline takes over.

You can also use download and keep searching to queue a result without closing the modal — see Click to Download.

DC++ rows re-arm on a new search

For GetComics and Usenet, a queued row stays locked for the rest of your visit, so you can't send the same release twice. DC++ is the exception: its result tokens belong to a single live search instance and are re-minted every time you search. Re-running a search gives DC++ results brand-new tokens, so those rows come back armed.

Nothing breaks if you grab the same bundle twice — AirDC++ recognizes it — but the row will not remember that you already took it.

docs.title: Adding AirDC++
docs.text:
You add AirDC++ from the Download Clients tab in Settings, the same place Usenet clients live.

Settings → Download Clients, with an AirDC++ client configured alongside an active SABnzbd.

AirDC++ does not deactivate your Usenet client

Download clients now belong to a group — usenet or dcpp — and the "only one active client" rule is scoped per group. Activating AirDC++ leaves SABnzbd or NZBGet active and untouched. See Download & API Settings.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Meaning Example Host Hostname or IP where the AirDC++ Web Client is running. 192.168.1.10 or airdcpp Port The AirDC++ Web Client port. 5600 Use SSL Tick if your instance is served over HTTPS. unticked URL Base Optional path prefix, if AirDC++ sits behind a reverse proxy on a subpath. /airdcpp Username An AirDC++ Web Client user with API access. clu Password That user's password. Target Directory Where AirDC++ should write completed bundles, expressed the way AirDC++ sees it. /downloads/comics/ Local Target Directory That same folder, expressed the way CLU sees it. /downloads/comics Hub URLs Optional. Restrict searches to specific hubs; leave empty to search every connected hub.

docs.title: Two different paths
docs.text:
Two different paths

Target Directory and Local Target Directory point at the same folder on disk, but they are written from two different points of view — and they are usually not the same string.

  • Target Directory is the path AirDC++ uses to write the file. AirDC++ receives this value and hands it to its own filesystem.
  • Local Target Directory is the path CLU uses to find that file afterwards, so it can move it into WATCH.

AirDC++ normally runs natively on the host or in its own container, so its filesystem is not CLU's filesystem. If you enter CLU's path in both boxes, AirDC++ will write somewhere CLU cannot see — or somewhere that does not exist — and downloads will complete but never reach your library.

The fix is a shared volume: map the folder AirDC++ downloads into your CLU container (in CLU's docker-compose.yml), then put the AirDC++-side path in Target Directory and the CLU-side path in Local Target Directory. Using CLU's existing WATCH folder for both sides is a perfectly good option if you can mount it into AirDC++.

docs.title: Test Connection
docs.text:
Click Test Connection after entering your details. CLU calls the instance live and reports a readable result.

Result Meaning What to check Connected CLU reached AirDC++, authenticated, and could open the local target directory. Nothing — you're good. Could not connect Nothing answered at that host/port. Host, port, SSL setting, and that AirDC++ is reachable from CLU's container. Authentication failed AirDC++ answered but rejected the credentials. Username and password. Non-JSON response Something answered, but it wasn't the AirDC++ API. You are probably pointed at the wrong port, a reverse proxy, or a login page. Timed out No response in time. Network path, firewall, or an overloaded instance. Target Directory is not a valid path on the AirDC++ host The path shape doesn't match the host's separator. See Path separators below. CLU cannot see '…' The Local Target Directory isn't a real directory inside CLU's container. Your volume mapping — the folder AirDC++ downloads into has to be mounted into CLU.

Test Connection tests what's on screen

Test Connection validates the values currently in the form, not the last saved configuration. You can correct a field and verify the fix before committing it.

docs.title: Path separators
docs.text:
AirDC++ does not reject a target directory it cannot parse — it silently folds the whole path into the filename. On a Windows host, / is a forbidden filename character rather than a separator, so a POSIX target directory like /downloads/temp/ turns a grab into a single file called _downloads_temp_Farmhouse 007.cbr sitting in AirDC++'s own default download folder. A Windows-style path on a Linux host fails the same way.

CLU reads the host's actual separator from the instance and refuses a target directory it can't parse, with a message naming the fix, rather than letting it through and producing mangled filenames.

CLU also appends the trailing separator AirDC++ expects, so you don't have to — /downloads/comics and /downloads/comics/ both work.

Change the path, re-test

Because this check depends on the AirDC++ host's own separator, it can only be validated against a live instance. Re-run Test Connection any time you change either directory.

docs.title: Status & Restart Recovery
docs.text: DC++ bundles appear on the Download Status page in the same table as direct and Usenet downloads, with live progress, the current stage, and byte counts.

docs.title: Job states
docs.text:
State What it means Does it clear itself? Downloading AirDC++ is transferring the bundle. Percentage and byte counts update as it goes. Yes — it moves on when the bundle finishes or fails. Complete The bundle finished and CLU moved it into WATCH. The folder monitor owns it from here. Yes — the row resolves itself and is dropped from the recovery ledger. Complete (not moved) The bundle finished, but CLU could not find the file to move it. Almost always a Local Target Directory problem. No. It stays until you dismiss it. Failed AirDC++ reported the download as failed. No. It stays until you dismiss it.

Failed and not-moved rows persist deliberately

Failed and Complete (not moved) rows survive a restart and stay on the page until you dismiss them by hand.

This is intentional. Both states mean a human needs to look — a failed grab needs re-trying from another source, and a not-moved bundle means a finished file is sitting somewhere CLU can't reach. Auto-purging them would let a restart silently swallow exactly the jobs worth knowing about.

Clean completions are the opposite: those are genuinely resolved, so they clear themselves.

docs.title: Restart recovery
docs.text:
New in v6.3

DC++ jobs survive a container restart. This is new in v6.3.

AirDC++ runs as its own process and keeps downloading whether CLU is up or not. Previously CLU tracked bundles in memory only, so a restart orphaned an in-flight job outright: the bundle vanished from the Status page and the import step never ran, leaving a finished file sitting in the download folder forever.

CLU now writes each job to a database ledger at grab time — before polling starts, so a crash in between can't lose the record — and clears the row when the job resolves cleanly.

What this buys you:

  • An in-flight bundle survives a restart. It reappears on the Status page and resumes being tracked.
  • A bundle that completed while CLU was down can still be imported. The last known target path is stored, so CLU knows where to look even if AirDC++ has already dropped the finished bundle from its queue.

Recovery at startup is deliberately database-only, so booting CLU is never held up waiting on network calls to AirDC++. The reconcile against the live AirDC++ queue happens on the poller's first round, a second or two later.

docs.title: Bundles you queued directly in AirDC++
docs.text:
The Status page also shows bundles you queued yourself, inside AirDC++, rather than through CLU. These are read-only.

CLU will never move these files

A bundle CLU didn't queue has no series, issue, or destination attached to it — CLU has no idea what it is. It is shown so the page reflects reality, but CLU will never move it into WATCH or import it.

If you want a hub download filed into your library, grab it through CLU's search modal rather than directly in AirDC++.

docs.title: Usenet doesn't have this yet
docs.text:
Usenet doesn't have this yet

The recovery ledger currently covers DC++ only. Usenet jobs are still tracked in memory, so a restart mid-download can still orphan one. This is a known follow-up rather than an oversight — better documented than discovered.

docs.title: Directory Features
docs.text:
Directory-based features provide batch operations across entire folders in your comic library. Instead of processing files individually, you can execute format conversions, filename cleanup, metadata updates, and sequence audits across an entire folder with a single action.

When browsing your library in the File Manager, directory operations are accessible via the menu to the right of any directory name.

docs.title: Available Directory Features
docs.text: Feature Description Documentation Rename All Files Standardizes filenames, strips redundant tags, and applies custom naming schemes. Rename All Files Convert Directory Batch converts CBR and RAR archives into standard CBZ files. Convert Directory Rebuild All Files Unpacks and rebuilds all archives (CBR, RAR, CBZ) to repair corrupted structures. Rebuild All Files Convert PDF to CBZ Extracts raster pages from PDF documents and repackages them into CBZ archives. Convert PDF to CBZ Missing Issue Check Scans issue number sequences to detect missing issues in a series. Missing Issue Check Enhance Images Applies automated contrast and curve adjustments across all pages in a folder. Enhance Images Bulk ComicInfo Actions Updates or removes embedded ComicInfo.xml metadata across all folder files. Update ComicInfo.xml

docs.title: Convert Directory
docs.text:
The Convert Directory tool batch converts all CBR and RAR comic archives within a directory into standard CBZ (ZIP) archives.

To run this tool, open the File Manager, click the menu to the right of any directory name, and select Convert CBR $\rightarrow$ CBZ.

This operation automatically skips any files that are already in CBZ format. If you need to re-pack or repair existing CBZ archives as well, use Rebuild All Files.

docs.title: Converting Subdirectories
docs.text:
By default, this feature converts only the files directly within the selected directory and does not recurse into subdirectories.

You can enable recursive processing by turning on Enable Subdirectories for Conversion in File Settings.

Performance considerations

Converting high-level directories containing hundreds of archives can require significant processing time and temporary disk space. Conversions run in the background with live progress reported in the operations indicator.

docs.title: A CBR left beside its own CBZ
docs.text:
Upon completing a conversion, CLU validates the newly created CBZ file and deletes the source CBR or RAR archive from disk.

If you encounter duplicate pairs (.cbr and .cbz with the same name) in your folders:

  • This typically indicates that an earlier conversion operation was interrupted before file cleanup completed, or that file system permissions on a network share (such as CIFS/SMB mounts) temporarily prevented source file deletion.
  • Verify that the resulting .cbz file opens and reads correctly, and safely delete the redundant .cbr source file.

docs.title: Enhance Images
docs.text:
When browsing your library in the File Manager or Collection, select Enhance Images from the folder menu to optimize visual clarity across all comic issues in that directory.

Older digital comic releases and vintage print scans can suffer from washed-out colors, elevated black levels, and dull contrast. The Enhance Images tool processes all images within each CBZ archive in the directory, improving readability while preserving subtle artistic details. This operation does not traverse subdirectories.

docs.title: Visual Comparison
docs.text: Before After

docs.title: Enhancement Algorithm
docs.text: Rather than applying a simple linear contrast adjustment — which risks blowing out paper highlights or clipping dark textures — CLU applies an intelligent modified S-curve adjustment using Python's Pillow (PIL) library.

docs.title: Modified S-Curve LUT
docs.text:
• Dark Tones (< 128 brightness): Receives the full S-curve adjustment, deepening muddy darks into rich blacks.
  • Bright Tones (≥ 128 brightness): Progressively blends the original pixel values with the curve, ensuring bright backgrounds, white panels, and text balloons do not get blown out.
  • Mid-Tones: Boosts color saturation and ink line sharpness without introducing harsh artifacts.
def modified_s_curve_lut():
    lut = []
    for i in range(256):
        # Calculate base S-curve value using cosine
        s = 0.5 - 0.5 * math.cos(math.pi * (i / 255))
        s_val = 255 * s
        # Apply full curve below 128; blend smoothly with original above 128
        if i < 128:
            blend = 0.0
        else:
            blend = (i - 128) / (255 - 128)
        new_val = (1 - blend) * s_val + blend * i
        lut.append(int(round(new_val)))
    return lut

docs.title: Color Space Adaptability
docs.text:
The enhancement pipeline inspects each image's color space before applying the transformation:

  • Grayscale (L): Applies the 256-value lookup table directly to the luminance channel.
  • RGB Color (RGB): Replicates and applies the LUT across all three color channels simultaneously.
  • Alpha Transparency (RGBA): Splits color and alpha channels, applies the LUT to red, green, and blue channels, and recombines them while preserving alpha transparency intact.

docs.title: Missing Issue Check
docs.text:
The Missing Issue Check tool scans a folder and its subdirectories to identify gaps in issue numbering sequences, generating a report file named missing.txt.

You can run this tool from the folder actions menu () in either the File Manager or the Collection view by selecting Missing Issue Check.

docs.title: How Detection Works
docs.text:
The check evaluates numeric patterns in filenames across each directory:

  • Sequences are assumed to start at issue #1 (e.g. 01, 001) and progress sequentially up to the highest issue number present in that folder.
  • Any gaps found between issue 1 and the highest numbered issue are recorded in the report.
  • When more than 50 consecutive issues are missing (often seen when series switch to legacy numbering, e.g. jumping from issue #70 to #500), the report summarizes the gap as a range: 
    Series Name 071-499 (1998) [Total missing: 429]

Sample missing.txt output:

Directory: /data/Comics/Eternal Warrior/v1992
Eternal Warrior 008 (1992).cbz

Directory: /data/Comics/Harbinger/v1992
Harbinger 011 (1992).cbz

Directory: /data/Comics/X-O Manowar/v2012
X-O Manowar 005 (2012).cbz
X-O Manowar 006 (2012).cbz
X-O Manowar 007 (2012).cbz

docs.title: Ignored Terms and File Rules
docs.text: To avoid false-positive gap reports caused by annuals, preview editions, or trade paperbacks, customize ignored terms and file patterns in System Settings under Missing Issue Configuration.

docs.title: Accessing missing.txt
docs.text:
The resulting missing.txt report is saved directly inside the scanned directory.

You can open and read missing.txt directly within the CLU interface by clicking the file card in the browser:

docs.title: Convert PDF to CBZ
docs.text: The Convert PDF to CBZ tool extracts raster images from PDF documents in a directory and packages them into standard CBZ archives. This makes digital comic magazines, art books, and graphic novels stored in PDF format fully compatible with comic readers, OPDS feeds, and metadata taggers.

docs.title: How to Run
docs.text:
1. Open the File Manager and locate the directory containing your PDF files.
  2. Click the menu to the right of the directory name.
  3. Select Convert PDF to CBZ from the dropdown menu.

docs.title: Conversion Process
docs.text:
• Page Extraction: Each page of the PDF document is rendered and extracted into a full-resolution image.
  • Archive Creation: Extracted pages are organized with standard zero-padded numbering (e.g. 001.jpg, 002.jpg) and compressed into a .cbz archive matching the source document's base filename.
  • Preserves Original Files: The conversion process verifies the newly created .cbz archive before finishing.

Once converted to CBZ, the issues can be read in the built-in Comic Reader, enhanced with Image Enhancement, or tagged with metadata using Fetch Metadata.

docs.title: Rebuild All Files
docs.text:
The Rebuild All Files tool unpacks, validates, and repackages all comic archives in a directory into standardized CBZ format.

While Convert Directory only processes CBR and RAR files and skips existing CBZ archives, Rebuild All Files processes every archive in the directory:

  1. Converts RAR / CBR files into clean CBZ format.
  2. Re-packs existing CBZ files, restructuring internal folder hierarchies, stripping non-image junk files, and repairing damaged zip headers.

Rebuilding fixes common indexing failures and thumbnail rendering errors encountered in media servers and comic readers.

docs.title: Archive Format Recovery
docs.text:
Archives are occasionally misnamed — for instance, a RAR archive incorrectly labeled with a .cbz extension. During rebuild operations, CLU inspects the archive's actual file headers. If standard ZIP extraction fails, CLU automatically tests RAR extraction, recovers the embedded page images, and repacks them into a true, valid CBZ archive.

To convert PDF documents into CBZ format, see Convert PDF to CBZ.

docs.title: Rename All Files
docs.text:
The Rename All Files tool standardizes and cleans filenames across all comics in a directory and its subdirectories. It is accessed via the icon to the right of any directory name in the File Manager.

When executed, the renaming engine applies the following cleaning rules:

  1. Removes all parenthetical metadata with the exception of the 4-digit release year (if present).
  2. Removes release format tags such as c2c (cover-to-cover).
  3. Strips bracketed annotations (e.g. [any text]) along with the brackets themselves.
  4. Trims scanner watermarks and trailing metadata appearing after {Series} {Issue} ({Year}).
  5. Removes duplicate whitespace and trailing spaces before the file extension.

The default naming pattern is: {Series Name} {Issue Number} ({Year})

You can configure custom naming formats in File Settings.

docs.title: Issue Number Handling
docs.text:
The renaming engine includes built-in rules for edge cases:

  • Configurable leading zeros: The Issue Number Leading Zeros setting controls issue padding: None (44), 3 digits (044, default), or 4 digits (0044).
  • Decimal and suffix issues: Point issues (e.g. 001.1) and publisher event tags (e.g. 1.MU, .NOW, and .INH) are preserved during renaming.
  • Large issue numbers: High issue numbers (such as DC #1,000,000 one-shots like Action Comics 1000000) are preserved without truncation.

docs.title: Batched Bulk Renames
docs.text:
Renaming directories with large file counts executes as a single, coalesced background task. Progress updates in real time via the operations indicator in the top navigation bar.

Batch renames run on a shared file job queue alongside post-move tagging, Remove XML, and bulk metadata tasks:

  • Jobs run sequentially in the order submitted, ensuring a rename operation never moves a file while a tagging job is active.
  • If another file operation is running, the rename dialog indicates that the job is queued and will start automatically once the current job finishes.

docs.title: Renaming Rules & Year Parsing
docs.text: Renaming rules are configured in rename_rules.ini on a priority basis. The default rule definitions are maintained in the project repository.

docs.title: Bare-Year Filenames
docs.text:
Filenames containing unparenthesized release years (such as Star Wars - Poe Dameron 001 2016) are parsed correctly, ensuring the four-digit year is not mistakenly captured as the issue number. When an archive lacks a ComicInfo.xml tag, the {issue_year} token falls back to the year extracted from the filename.

Resolving collision suffixes

If files in a folder previously acquired collision suffixes (such as Series (2).cbz, Series (3).cbz), simply re-run Rename All Files on that folder to re-parse the archives and restore their proper issue numbers.

docs.title: Bulk Actions on ComicInfo.xml
docs.text: CLU lets you manage your ComicInfo.xml metadata in bulk with two primary operations: Update and Delete.

docs.title: Bulk Update ComicInfo
docs.text:
This tool allows you to batch-update key metadata values in the ComicInfo.xml file of each CBZ archive in a directory.

Four fields can be updated simultaneously:

  • Series: Updates the Series Name across all files in the directory.
  • Issue: Updates the Issue Number across all files in the directory.
  • Volume: Updates the Volume / Year field across all files in the directory.
  • Publisher: Updates the Publisher name across all files in the directory.

docs.title: Bulk Delete ComicInfo
docs.text: This tool strips the embedded ComicInfo.xml file from multiple archives at once. It can be executed from either the Library View or the File Browser:

docs.title: Library View (Multi-Select)
docs.text: In the Library grid, hold CTRL or SHIFT while clicking files to select multiple items. Once two or more files are selected, the Bulk Actions Bar appears at the bottom of the screen. Click Remove XML to remove the metadata file from every selected archive.

docs.title: File Browser (Folder Menu)
docs.text: When navigating via the File Browser, click the menu on any folder and select Remove All XML. CLU will remove the ComicInfo.xml file from all comic archives contained within that directory.

docs.title: Job Queue Behavior
docs.text:
Bulk metadata deletions run on the shared file job queue:

  • If another file operation (such as batch renaming or metadata scraping) is currently running, the job is queued and begins automatically when preceding jobs finish.
  • Files that do not contain a ComicInfo.xml are recorded as skipped rather than errors.
  • A corrupted or locked archive will not halt processing for the remainder of the files in the batch.

docs.title: File Downloads
docs.text:
Install the Chrome Extension, configure it and then visit GetComics.info to right-click and download files directly to your server.

Extensions for Edge and Firefox have been submitted and are awaiting approval.

docs.title: Supported Sites
docs.text:
Currently, GetComics.org and Comic Book Plus are supported for downloads.

As you browse these sites and find a book you'd like to read, v2 of the extension will append a CLU icon next to the supported download link(s).

Click to send to CLU

Clicking this will send the download request to CLU and you'll see it show up in the download status page.

Some older style links may not have the icon appended. In this case, you can right click one of the supported download providers and you should see Send to CLU in your context menu

Send download to CLU

You can then navigate to the Download Status page in CLU (http://localhost/status) and watch the progress of the file download

docs.title: Supported Providers
docs.text: All supported providers are free tier only and currently do not support login or credentials.

docs.title: GetComics.Org
docs.text: Indicated by Red Download Now and Blue Mirror Download buttons.

docs.title: Pixeldrain
docs.text: Indicated by the Pixeldrain button

docs.title: Mega.nz
docs.text: Indicated by the Mega button

docs.title: Comic Book +
docs.text: When logged in and browsing https://comicbookplus.com, right-click on the "Download File" link

docs.title: The Search Modal
docs.text: Separately from the browser extension, CLU has a source-search modal you open from inside the app — on a series page, the Wanted Issues page, and the Reading Lists page. It queries every configured download source at once: GetComics, Usenet, and DC++, each under its own section header ordered by Source Priority.

docs.title: Queue more than one at a time
docs.text:
New in v6.3

Every result now has two buttons: download, or download and keep searching.

Clicking a result used to queue it and close the modal, which made queuing a terminal action — so spotting a second or third file you wanted meant reopening the modal and re-running the entire search for each one.

Button What it does Download Queues the release and closes the modal. The original behavior. Download and keep searching Queues the release and leaves the modal open, so you can carry on browsing the same result set.

docs.title: Duplicate protection
docs.text:
Because the grab endpoints aren't idempotent, keeping the modal open needs protection against sending the same release twice:

  • Both buttons in a row lock together while a grab is in flight. Otherwise the second button stays live and the same release gets sent twice.
  • Queued rows stay locked for the visit. Narrowing your query and re-searching brings already-taken rows back locked rather than arming them again.

DC++ is the exception

DC++ result tokens belong to a single live search instance and are re-minted on every search, so DC++ rows re-arm when you run a new search. They can't be matched back to what you already queued. See DC++ Searching & Grabbing.

docs.title: Downloading the right comic
docs.text:
Fixed in v6.5 — CLU downloaded a comic you didn't ask for

This is the most consequential fix in the release, and it's worth describing by its symptom, because that's what people searched for.

A GetComics listing page — a weekly update post, a Top-10 roundup — holds many unrelated comics. CLU used to fetch the first download link on the page, whatever it was aiming for. So a run of wanted issues could all quietly download the same unrelated comic, each one filed under the name of the issue it was supposed to be.

A download of the wrong comic under the right name is worse than no download, because nothing looks broken until you open it. CLU now takes the specific entry it was after, or nothing at all.

docs.title: Posts split into several downloads
docs.text: A GetComics post is often split into parts — "#1–15", "#16–30", "#31–50". CLU used to take the first part regardless of which issue it wanted. The correct part is now picked per issue.

docs.title: One sweep at a time
docs.text:
If a scheduled download run is already in progress, Run Now and the next scheduled trigger stand down rather than starting a second copy that re-queues everything the first run is still working through.

Check for Missing Issues is the exception

A full sweep does not block the per-series Check for Missing Issues button.

Clicking that is an explicit request about one series, and making you wait out a multi-hour sweep would be worse than the single duplicate download it can occasionally cost.

docs.title: A sweep queues at most 150 downloads
docs.text:
This is a blast-radius limit, not a throughput limit. Hitting it stops that run; the rest is picked up on the next one.

Worth knowing so that hitting the cap doesn't look like data loss — nothing has been dropped or forgotten, it's just been deferred.

docs.title: A rate-limited host is stood down
docs.text:
When a host starts refusing requests, CLU now stops asking it for a while instead of asking again on every queued item.

MEGA in particular used to produce dozens of identical "Too many requests" failures against a handful of files, burning the queue without downloading anything.

A cooling host is moved to the back of the list, not dropped — so it's still used when it's the only link a post offers.

docs.title: Chrome Extension
docs.text:
Extension Image

Once you have the Chrome extension installed, you will need to configure the options.

You'll see a screen similar to this within Chrome.

Extension Settings

docs.title: API URL
docs.text:
Visiting https://localhost/download will show you a confirmation that your API url is running and ready to accept requests.

In order to accept requests from machines other than the one running CLU, you will need to have a tunnel, domain, VPN or other means of access setup.

Personally, I use Cloudflare tunnels and to accommodate authenticating that way, you can pass custom content in the header with the download request.

docs.title: Custom Headers
docs.text:
This setting allows you to pass custom auth variables or anything else in the header. Simplay enter the content you need to pass as JSON. The example provided shows you how to pass Client ID and Client Secret to authenticate to your site.

{
    "CF-Access-Client-Id":"you-client-id",
    "CF-Access-Client-Secret":"your-secret"
}
