docs.text: Click Change Location to re-map the series to a different folder. CLU updates the stored mapping and reconciles your files.

docs.title: API Sync
docs.text: Click API Sync to query the Metron API for new issue solicitations, publication date updates, and revised series descriptions. This sync runs automatically every night across all subscribed series.

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text: Click Refresh to purge local caches, refetch the latest series and issue records from Metron (including newly added creator credits), and rescan your local storage folder to reconcile file matches.

docs.title: Monitor
docs.text:
The Monitor toggle controls whether CLU actively tracks and searches for missing issues:

  • When Monitored: Missing issues appear on the Wanted page and are included in nightly automated download sweeps (GetComics, Usenet, DC++).
  • When Not Monitored: The series is greyed out on the Pull List, and automated downloader searches are paused.

Turn off monitoring for completed runs where you already own all desired issues, or when remaining issues are out-of-print and unavailable.

docs.title: On the Stack
docs.text: Enable On the Stack to allow this series to surface its next unread issue in the On the Stack carousel on your Collection homepage.

docs.title: Issue Statuses: Wanted, Owned, and Skipped
docs.text:
Each issue in the series checklist carries a tracking status:

  • Owned: Issues physically detected in your mapped folder, or issues you manually marked as owned (e.g. issues collected in an omnibus or trade paperback).
  • Wanted: Released issues that are absent from your local folder. These are automatically included in automated download sweeps.
  • Skipped: Issues you do not wish to collect. Skipped issues are excluded from download searches.

docs.title: Multi-Select Actions
docs.text:
Select multiple issues using the checkboxes to perform bulk status updates:

  • Mark as Owned: Manually mark the selected issues as collected.
  • Mark as Skipped: Exclude selected issues from search sweeps.
  • Mark as Wanted: Re-enable tracking for issues previously marked as Owned or Skipped.

docs.title: Wanted
docs.text:
The Wanted page tracks all absent and upcoming issues across your subscribed series and bookmarked reading lists.

The top toolbar provides three global actions:

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text: Re-scans all series on your Pull List to recalculate wanted and missing counts based on your active library files.

docs.title: Scan Download Directory
docs.text: Scans your download directory to detect and process any newly completed files deposited since the last pass.

docs.title: Check for Missing Issues
docs.text:
Manually initiates an automated search sweep for wanted issues across all enabled download sources (GetComics, Usenet, and DC++), ranked according to your configured Source Priority.

Active sweeps report progress directly into the Active Operations indicator in the top navigation bar. If a scheduled sweep is already in progress, additional triggers stand down to avoid redundant concurrent requests.

docs.title: Missing Issues
docs.text: The Missing Issues section lists all uncollected issues whose official Store Date has already passed, ordered chronologically from oldest to newest.

docs.title: Search for Missing Issues
docs.text:
You can search for any missing issue across your download providers directly within CLU:

  1. Click the Search button next to any missing issue.

  1. A unified search modal opens, querying GetComics, Usenet indexers, and DC++ concurrently. Results are grouped by source under prioritized section headers.
  2. If necessary, adjust search keywords to refine queries for difficult-to-find titles:

  1. Click the Download button on any result to dispatch the file to your download client.

docs.title: From Reading Lists
docs.text:
The From Reading Lists section displays missing issues sourced from tracked reading lists.

This section appears whenever Track Wanted is toggled on for at least one reading list. Unmatched entries in tracked lists are treated as wanted issues and queried during automated nightly download sweeps.

Column Description Series The series title recorded in the reading list. Issue The issue number required by the list. Year The publication year (if recorded by the source list). Reading List The source reading list containing the missing entry. Actions Single-click search across your configured download sources.

docs.title: Search Logic for Reading List Entries
docs.text:
• Back-catalogue entries without dates: Unlike future series solicitations (which wait for an announced store date before searching), reading list entries lacking a publication year are presumed to be released back-catalogue issues and are actively searched.
  • 7-Day Cooldown: If an issue download fails or cannot be unpacked, CLU applies a 7-day cooldown to prevent re-downloading the same broken archive every night.
  • Invalid entries excluded: Entries with missing series names or blank issue numbers are automatically excluded from search sweeps.
  • Instant sync: Mapping a missing file by hand removes it from this section immediately, and clearing a mapping restores it.

docs.title: Upcoming Issues
docs.text: The Upcoming Issues section lists future releases for your subscribed series, ordered by their announced Store Date. Once an issue's store date arrives, it automatically transitions into the Missing Issues list if it has not yet been acquired.

docs.title: Weekly Packs
docs.text:
If you prefer downloading entire publisher release bundles rather than managing individual issues, the Weekly Packs feature automatically checks for and downloads weekly release packs.

Weekly Packs Disables Individual Auto-Downloads

Enabling Weekly Packs disables individual-issue automated downloads in CLU. Weekly packs provide comprehensive coverage for chosen publishers, replacing daily per-issue sweeps.

docs.title: Supported Publishers
docs.text:
Weekly packs are available for the following publisher categories:

  • Marvel
  • DC Comics
  • Image Comics
  • Dark Horse Comics
  • Indie (covers all independent and small-press publishers)

Select one or more publishers to include their release bundles in your download schedule.

docs.title: Download Options
docs.text:
Configure the scheduling and retrieval settings for weekly pack downloads:

Option Description Check Day Day of the week to begin checking for newly released weekly packs. Check Time Time of day to initiate the availability check. Start Date The starting date for pack downloads (supports up to 6 months of historical packs). Retry Option Automatically retries daily if the weekly pack has not yet been uploaded. Save Settings Saves configuration changes and updates the background schedule. Check & Download Immediately initiates a check and downloads the latest pack if available. Check Pack Status Queries download sources to check whether the latest pack is released without downloading.

docs.title: Execution Status
docs.text: The status panel reports the Last Run timestamp, Next Scheduled Run, and the date of the Last Successful Pack retrieved.

docs.title: Recent Downloads
docs.text:
The recent downloads table tracks historical pack acquisitions:

Column Description Pack Date Official release date of the weekly pack. Publisher Publisher category of the pack. Format Image format of the comics contained in the pack (JPG or WEBP). Status Ingestion status (Success, Processing, or Failed). Downloaded Timestamp recording when the pack was successfully retrieved.

docs.title: Single File Features
docs.text: Single file features provide targeted operations for individual comic files. Accessible directly from the action menu across the Collection, File Manager, and Source Wall views, these tools let you inspect, repair, crop, or enhance specific issues without running batch jobs across entire directories.

docs.title: Available Single File Features
docs.text: Feature Description Documentation Edit CBZ File Visually reorder pages, upload replacement covers, crop artwork, and remove junk files. Edit CBZ File Single File Rebuild Repair corrupted archive headers and convert individual CBR or RAR files to CBZ. Single File Rebuild Crop Cover Automatically split a wraparound cover, isolating the front cover as the primary image. Crop Cover Remove First Image Delete unwanted lead pages, scanner watermark cards, or advertisement splash screens. Remove First Image Add Blank Image Append a trailing blank image to fix two-page spread alignment in manga readers. Add Blank Image Enhance Images Apply automated contrast and curve adjustments across all pages in a single issue. Enhance Images Add Read Date Manually log or update the date an issue was read to enrich reading statistics. Add Read Date Delete File Remove a single issue from disk, with soft-delete recovery via the Trash Can. Delete File

docs.title: Add Blank Image
docs.text:
Accessible in the File Manager via the menu on any comic card.

In two-page spread and dual-page reader modes (such as Komga, Kavita, or desktop comic viewers), pages are rendered side-by-side in pairs. If a comic or manga volume has an odd number of pages, or lacks an alignment spacer, every subsequent two-page spread throughout the book can become misaligned.

The Add Blank Image tool inserts a blank image (zzzz9999.png) at the very end of the CBZ archive. This evens out the page count, ensuring dual-page layouts and splash spreads display across matching panels without modifying story content.

docs.title: Crop Cover
docs.text:
Accessible from the menu on any comic card in the File Manager or Collection view.

Many digital releases feature a two-page wraparound spread as the first image in the archive (combining the back cover, spine, and front cover into a single wide image). This can cause readers and thumbnail generators to display the entire spread or the back cover instead of the front cover.

The Crop Cover tool automatically fixes this layout:

  • Isolates the front cover: Crops the right-hand half of the lead image and sets it as the primary cover (00a.jpg).
  • Preserves the original spread: The uncropped wraparound image is retained and repositioned as the second page (00b.jpg), ensuring no artwork is lost.
Before (Full Wraparound Spread) After (Isolated Front Cover)

For tri-fold covers or freeform cropping, use the interactive crop tools available in Edit CBZ File.

docs.title: Add Read Date
docs.text:
Accessible only in the Collection view via the menu on any comic card.

While CLU automatically records reading dates when comics are read through the built-in reader, Add Read Date lets you manually record or adjust the completion date for issues read outside the browser.

Logged reading dates feed directly into the reading activity charts, timelines, and annual reading heatmaps on the Library Insights page.

docs.title: Delete File
docs.text:
Accessible in the File Manager via the icon, or in the Collection view via the menu on any comic card.

The Delete File utility removes an individual comic issue from disk. A confirmation dialog displays the target file name to prevent accidental removals:

docs.title: Soft-Delete & Trash Can Protection
docs.text:
If the Trash Can is enabled in settings, deleted files are moved to /cache/trash rather than being permanently destroyed, allowing you to restore them if deleted by mistake.

See File Management: Delete & Trash for full details on recovery and size-based trash eviction.

docs.title: Edit CBZ File
docs.text:
When viewing an issue in the File Manager or Collection, click the menu and select Edit File (or Edit CBZ) to open the in-browser archive editor.

CLU unpacks the archive into an isolated temporary workspace and loads the pages into an interactive visual grid:

From this interface, you can perform several operations:

docs.title: Rename and Reorder Pages
docs.text:
Click on any filename to edit it inline. Press ENTER to save the new name. Pages automatically re-sort in the grid according to alphanumeric ordering.

For example, updating a filename to 00b.jpg causes it to sort immediately after 00a.jpg:

docs.title: Upload New or Replacement Pages
docs.text:
You can drag and drop image files directly into the editor to add missing pages or replace corrupted covers:

  1. Locate your replacement cover image and drag it into the editor modal.

  1. The image is uploaded, scaled to match the dimensions of the other pages in the archive, and inserted into alphanumeric order.

Allowed Image Formats

Only image files are permitted inside the archive (.jpg, .jpeg, .png, .gif, .webp, .bmp). Non-image files will be rejected upon upload.

  1. Once the replacement image is inserted, delete the old or damaged cover image and save changes.

docs.title: Crop Images
docs.text:
The built-in crop tool provides precise controls for isolating panel artwork or cover sections from multi-page spreads:

  • <-| Left: Crops and saves the left half of the image as the new cover. The original full spread is retained and repositioned as the second image in the archive.
  • Right |->: Crops the image to the right half and assigns it as the primary cover.
  • Middle: Extracts the center panel for tri-fold covers.
  • Free Crop: Allows click-and-drag freeform cropping directly on the canvas:
    • Click and drag to define the crop area.
    • Hold SPACE to reposition the selection box.
    • Hold SHIFT to lock standard comic page aspect ratios.

Preserves Original Images

Crop operations preserve the original un-cropped spread inside the archive, ensuring you can undo an accidental crop by removing the cropped page and restoring the original.

docs.title: Delete Pages
docs.text:
Click the icon on any page card to delete it from the archive. This is useful for stripping non-story pages, advertisements, or scanner promotional cards.

Immediate Deletion

Page deletions within the editor take effect immediately upon confirmation.

docs.title: Save Changes
docs.text: Click Save to repack the archive and clean up temporary files.

docs.title: Automated Junk File Cleanup
docs.text: In File Settings, you can configure specific file extensions to be automatically purged whenever a CBZ is edited (e.g. .nfo, .sfv, .db, .DS_Store). Non-image metadata files such as ComicInfo.xml are automatically preserved during repacking.

docs.title: Enhance Images
docs.text:
Accessible from the menu on any comic card in the File Manager or Collection view.

Vintage print scans and older digital comic releases often suffer from faded ink, elevated gray black-levels, and washed-out colors. The Enhance Images tool applies a non-destructive image curve optimization across every page in the selected CBZ archive, enriching contrast and color vibrancy while preserving bright paper highlights and fine line art.

docs.title: Visual Comparison
docs.text:
Before After

For a full technical breakdown of the modified S-curve algorithm and color space handling, see Directory Features: Enhance Images.

docs.title: Single File Rebuild
docs.text:
Accessible from the menu on any comic card in the File Manager or Collection view.

Single File Rebuild performs two primary functions:

  1. Repairs existing CBZ files: Unpacks and repackages the archive to resolve zip header errors, strip internal folder clutter, and repair archives that fail to open in comic readers.
  2. Converts CBR / RAR to CBZ: Re-packs single RAR-compressed files into standardized CBZ archives.

docs.title: Automated Error Recovery
docs.text:
During a rebuild, CLU unpacks the archive into an isolated staging directory and validates the contents before replacing the original file.

If extraction fails (for example, if the archive is encrypted or truncated), CLU automatically aborts the operation, leaves your original comic file untouched, and logs the detailed error on the Problem Files page under the Rebuild category.

Container Repairs vs. Corrupt Image Data

Rebuilding repairs the archive container, not corrupted image data. It successfully recovers archives misnamed with the wrong extension (such as a RAR file labeled as .cbz) or broken zip directory headers. However, if the underlying image files inside the archive suffer from CRC corruption, rebuilding cannot restore damaged pixels.

For severely corrupted files, use Find a replacement directly from its row on the Problem Files page.

docs.title: Remove First Image
docs.text:
Accessible from the menu on any comic card in the File Manager or Collection view.

Older comic releases and scans occasionally prepend a non-cover image to the beginning of the archive — such as a scanner credit card, watermarked logo, or advertising splash page. This causes library browsers to display the credit card rather than the real comic cover.

The Remove First Image tool unpacks the archive, permanently removes the first image file, and repacks the CBZ so page two becomes the new primary cover.

Before (Scanner Card First) After (True Cover Restored)

Permanent Deletion

Removing the first image is an immediate, irreversible operation. If you are unsure whether the first file is truly an extraneous scanner card or the actual cover, open the comic in the built-in reader or use Edit CBZ File to inspect and manage pages visually before deleting.

docs.title: Usenet Downloads
docs.text:
CLU supports downloading comics from Usenet (newsgroups) alongside Direct Downloads (GetComics) and DC++.

Configured from the Download Clients tab in Settings, the Usenet subsystem mirrors the modular design of CLU's metadata providers: you connect a download client, add one or more Newznab indexers, and assign Usenet a priority ranking in Source Priority.

docs.title: How It Fits Together
docs.text:
Usenet support consists of three core components:

Component Purpose Documentation Download Client The application that downloads articles and unpacks NZBs (SABnzbd or NZBGet). Adding a Download Client Indexers One or more Newznab indexers that CLU queries for comic releases. Adding Newznab Indexers Source Priority The priority ranking that determines whether Usenet, GetComics, or DC++ is searched first during automated sweeps. Source Priority

Once configured, Usenet integrates seamlessly into manual single-issue searches on the Series page, the Wanted Issues dashboard, and nightly automated download sweeps. See Searching & Grabbing for day-to-day workflows.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To use Usenet downloads, you need:

  • A Usenet Provider account (the news server containing binary articles that your download client connects to).
  • A Download Client (SABnzbd or NZBGet) running and reachable over the network by CLU.
  • At least one Newznab Indexer account with a valid API key.

Usenet Provider vs. Indexer

These represent two distinct services: - Your Usenet Provider stores and delivers binary data; server credentials are configured inside SABnzbd or NZBGet. - Your Indexer catalogs releases and provides searchable .nzb metadata; indexers and API keys are configured inside CLU.

docs.title: Adding Newznab Indexers
docs.text:
Indexers function as the search engines of Usenet. When searching for a missing comic, CLU queries your configured Newznab indexers for releases matching the wanted series and issue, then passes the matching .nzb release directly to your download client.

Indexers are configured in the Download Clients tab in Settings.

docs.title: Indexer Fields
docs.text:
Field Description Name A recognizable label for the indexer (e.g. Drunkenslug, Geek, NinjaCentral). URL The full base API URL for your indexer (e.g. https://api.indexer.com). API Key Your personal API key provided in your indexer account profile. Category The Newznab category ID to query. Defaults to standard comic category 7030. Priority Sets query precedence when multiple indexers are enabled (see below).

Comics Category ID

Newznab-compliant indexers universally standardize comic books under category ID 7030 (Books > Comics). Only alter this value if your specific indexer utilizes a custom non-standard categorization schema.

docs.title: Indexer Priority Ordering
docs.text:
When configuring multiple indexers, Priority determines the sequence in which indexers are queried and displayed:

  • Higher-priority indexers are searched first.
  • Results from higher-priority indexers are displayed first in manual search modals and automated queues.

Indexer priority is internal to your Usenet configuration. It works in conjunction with global Source Priority, which decides whether Usenet as a whole is queried before or after GetComics and DC++.

Search Visibility

Usenet results remain hidden in manual search modals and automated sweeps until at least one indexer has been configured and enabled with a valid API key.

docs.title: Searching & Grabbing
docs.text: Once you have configured an indexer and an active download client, Usenet is integrated across CLU's manual and automated search interfaces.

docs.title: Where Usenet Appears
docs.text:
• Series Page (Manual Search): When searching for a specific issue, CLU queries your enabled indexers alongside GetComics and DC++, ordering results according to your Source Priority.
  • Wanted Issues Dashboard: The combined search modal on the Wanted Issues page displays Usenet results under dedicated section headers with direct Download action buttons.
  • Automated Sweeps: The nightly wanted-issues sweep queries enabled indexers automatically based on your Source Priority ranking.

Activation Requirement

Usenet results only appear in search interfaces once at least one indexer is enabled. If indexers are active but no download client is configured, CLU displays a warning indicator so grabs do not silently fail.

docs.title: Grabbing a Release
docs.text:
When you click Download on a Usenet search result:

  1. CLU dispatches the release's NZB payload directly to your configured download client (SABnzbd or NZBGet).
  2. The download client verifies, repairs, and unpacks the binary articles, reporting live progress to CLU's Download Status dashboard.
  3. Completed comic files are transferred into your WATCH directory.
  4. The Folder Monitoring pipeline detects the new arrival, matches it against your wanted list, standardizes the filename, and moves the comic into your library.

Multipart and Obfuscated Usenet Releases

Usenet releases frequently arrive as nested split-volumes or multi-layer archives (e.g. .zip parts containing a .rar that wraps the comic). CLU's background pipeline automatically unwraps and extracts these archives layer-by-layer. See Auto-Unwrap for Hybrid & Multipart Releases.

docs.title: Ambiguous and Bare-Title Releases
docs.text:
Releases on Usenet that do not contain an identifiable issue number in their title (or consist solely of a bare series title) are treated with caution:

  • Manual Search: These releases remain visible in manual search modals so you can inspect and grab them if you recognize the release.
  • Automated Sweeps: Ambiguous releases without issue numbers are strictly excluded from automated auto-download sweeps, preventing false-positive grabs for unrelated annuals or one-shots.

docs.title: Adding a Download Client
docs.text:
Your download client (SABnzbd or NZBGet) is the dedicated application that receives NZB files from CLU, connects to your Usenet provider, downloads and verifies binary articles, and assembles the completed comic archives.

Download clients are added and managed from the Download Clients tab in Settings.

Client Group Scope

CLU supports one active client per client group: - You can configure credentials for both SABnzbd and NZBGet, but only the client currently toggled as active will receive grabs. - Usenet clients belong to a separate group from DC++ clients, allowing you to run an active Usenet client and an active AirDC++ client simultaneously.

docs.title: SABnzbd Configuration
docs.text: Field Description Host The hostname or IP address where SABnzbd is reachable (e.g. 192.168.1.50 or container hostname sabnzbd). Port The SABnzbd web interface port (default 8080). API Key Found in SABnzbd under Config > General > API Key. Category The SABnzbd category assigned to comic grabs (e.g. comics). Highly recommended so finished files land in your designated WATCH folder.

docs.title: NZBGet Configuration
docs.text: Field Description Host The hostname or IP address where NZBGet is reachable. Port The NZBGet web interface port (default 6789). Username The NZBGet control username (default nzbget). Password The NZBGet control password. Category The NZBGet category assigned to comic grabs (e.g. comics).

docs.title: Testing the Connection
docs.text:
After entering your client details, click Test Connection to verify network connectivity and authentication. CLU evaluates the connection and provides human-readable feedback:

Result Status Troubleshooting Action Connected Success Communication verified. Click Save to activate. Connection refused Failed Verify host IP/hostname, port number, and ensure the client is running. 401 / Unauthorized Failed Verify the API key (SABnzbd) or control username/password (NZBGet). Non-JSON response Failed Check that the port points to the API service rather than a reverse proxy or web portal. Timed out Timeout Check Docker network bridges, firewall rules, or host resource saturation.

docs.title: Source Priority
docs.text:
Source Priority governs how CLU prioritizes and queries its three supported download sources: Direct Downloads (GetComics), Usenet, and DC++.

Source Priority is configured from the Download Clients tab in Settings.

Each source features an On / Off toggle and a draggable handle to set priority order. You can enable any combination of sources according to your preferences (at least one source must remain active). Disabling a source temporarily removes it from auto-download sweeps without deleting its underlying client credentials.

docs.title: Automated Sweeps vs. Manual Search
docs.text:
Source Priority behaves differently depending on whether an operation is automated or manual:

Behavior Automated Sweeps Manual Search Modal Execution Order Sources are queried sequentially in ranked order. Results sections are displayed in ranked order. Source Membership Only enabled, ranked sources are queried. Unranked or disabled sources are skipped. All configured sources are queried, regardless of ranking or toggle state.

Ranking Governs Automated Sweeps

If a source is toggled off or omitted from your Source Priority ranking, nightly automated download sweeps will never query it — even if its credentials are fully configured.

In contrast, the manual search modal queries every configured service, ensuring you can always perform manual grabs from any provider by hand.

docs.title: Automated Download Cascading
docs.text:
During nightly automated sweeps, CLU processes wanted issues using a cascading priority check:

  1. Queries the highest-ranked enabled source for the wanted issue.
  2. If an acceptable match is found, CLU queues the download and stops searching — lower-ranked sources are skipped for that issue.
  3. If no acceptable match is found, CLU falls through to the next ranked source.
  4. If no enabled source produces a match, the issue remains wanted and is retried on the next run.

Only high-confidence releases matching the specific series, volume, and issue number are grabbed. Ambiguous releases without issue numbers are never auto-grabbed.

docs.title: Cascading Example
docs.text:
With a priority ranking of Usenet $\rightarrow$ GetComics $\rightarrow$ DC++:

Scenario Result Usenet returns a match Download queued from Usenet. GetComics and DC++ are skipped. Usenet has no match; GetComics returns a match Download queued from GetComics. DC++ is skipped. Usenet and GetComics have no match; DC++ returns a match Download queued from DC++. No source returns an acceptable match The issue remains wanted and is retried on the next sweep. DC++ configured but toggled off DC++ is skipped during automated sweeps, but remains searchable in manual modals.

docs.title: Search Modal Display
docs.text:
In single-issue search modals across the Series page, Wanted Issues, and Reading Lists, each source renders under its own labeled section header. Source Priority controls which section appears first at the top of the modal.

DC++ Search Timing

DC++ searches typically require 20–30 seconds because AirDC++ paces its hub queries to respect peer limits. Its section populates progressively after direct download and Usenet results appear. See DC++ Searching & Grabbing.

docs.title: Source Priority vs. Download Provider Priority
docs.text:
These two settings control different layers of the download architecture:

  • Source Priority (this page): Determines which source system (GetComics, Usenet, or DC++) to query first for an issue.
  • Download Provider Priority (in Download Settings): Orders the individual file hosting mirrors within GetComics results (e.g. Pixeldrain vs. Mediafire vs. Zippyshare). It has no effect on Usenet or DC++.

docs.title: Users & Access
docs.text:
New in v6.2

User accounts, roles, and per-library/per-folder grants arrived in v6.2. v6.3 added per-user themes and dashboard layouts.

CLU supports real user accounts so you can share your library with family or friends without handing over the keys to your settings, your file manager, or your downloads. Everyone gets their own reading history, favorites, and stats.

It is opt-in by design. If you run CLU on your own, nothing changes — there is still no login, and every screen works exactly as it did before.

docs.title: The two operating modes
docs.text:
CLU decides which mode to run in on its own. You never set it directly.

Mode When it applies What happens Implicit-owner mode (default) One account, and no CLU_USERNAME/CLU_PASSWORD environment gate. No login at all. Every request runs as the Store Owner. Role checks and library/folder scoping are skipped outright. Multi-user mode A second account exists, or the CLU_USERNAME/CLU_PASSWORD env gate is set. Login is required and enforcement activates everywhere — nav visibility, API routes, and path access.

Multi-user turns itself on

Creating your second account is what flips CLU into multi-user mode. There is no toggle to hunt for — and no way to be halfway there. See First Run & Logging In if you want to stay single-user.

docs.title: The three pieces
docs.text:
Piece What it controls Docs Accounts & roles What an account can do — browse, manage files, or change settings. Roles & Permissions Library grants Which libraries an account can see at all. Library & Folder Access Folder grants Which folders within a granted library an account can see. Library & Folder Access

Roles and grants are independent. A Clerk with no library grants sees no files; a Reader granted every library still can't reach Settings.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Roles & Permissions — the Reader → Clerk → Store Owner hierarchy and what each role unlocks.
  • First Run & Logging In — the one-time Store Owner Setup screen, and migrating the legacy CLU_USERNAME/CLU_PASSWORD env gate.
  • Managing Users — Settings → Users: adding, editing, deactivating, and deleting accounts.
  • Library & Folder Access — the two-layer grant model and exactly what each combination shows.
  • Per-User Data — what is now yours alone, and the two things that are still shared.
  • My Account — every user's own theme, dashboard layout, and API tokens.

docs.title: Store Owner Setup
docs.text:
On a fresh install CLU shows a one-time Store Owner Setup screen at /setup-owner. Pick a username and a password; that account becomes the Store Owner and, once it exists, the setup screen redirects home and never appears again.

You are not required to do anything else. With a single account and no environment gate, CLU stays in implicit-owner mode: no login screen, no role checks, no folder scoping.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
Once a second account exists — or the CLU_USERNAME/CLU_PASSWORD environment gate is set — CLU requires a login.

Passwords are stored using werkzeug hashing, never in plaintext. The session secret is persisted, so logging in survives a container restart rather than logging everyone out on every upgrade.

docs.title: Migrating the legacy CLU_USERNAME / CLU_PASSWORD gate
docs.text:
Older CLU installs used two environment variables as a simple password gate. Those still work, but they are no longer the mechanism — they are a seed.

At startup, CLU migrates those credentials into a real, hashed Store Owner account. The same username and password keep working, but now through the normal login screen, and the account can be edited, given tokens, and joined by other accounts like any other.

Setting the env gate forces multi-user mode

While CLU_USERNAME/CLU_PASSWORD are set, CLU runs in multi-user mode even with only one account. Remove them if you want the login-free experience back — see below.

See the Config Installation page for where these variables live in your Docker configuration.

docs.title: How to stay single-user
docs.text:
Implicit-owner mode is the default and requires nothing from you. To keep it:

  • Keep exactly one account.
  • Do not set CLU_USERNAME / CLU_PASSWORD.

docs.title: How to get back to no-login
docs.text:
If you tried multi-user and want the login-free experience back:

  1. Delete every account except the Store Owner (see Managing Users).
  2. Remove CLU_USERNAME and CLU_PASSWORD from your Docker environment, if set.
  3. Restart CLU.

Lost the only owner password?

The last active Store Owner is protected and cannot be demoted, deactivated, or deleted, so you cannot lock yourself out from inside the app. There is, however, no in-app password recovery — setting CLU_USERNAME/CLU_PASSWORD after an owner already exists does not reset it, because those variables only seed an owner when no account exists at all. Recovering a forgotten owner password means resetting it directly in the CLU database. Ask on Discord before you start.

docs.title: Changing a password
docs.text: Passwords are changed from Settings → Users by a Store Owner, including the owner's own — see Managing Users. The My Account page covers appearance, dashboard layout, and API tokens only.

docs.title: Library & Folder Access
docs.text:
Access is granted in two layers, so you can be as broad or as precise as you like.

  • Library grants are the outer gate — which libraries an account may see at all.
  • Folder grants refine access within a granted library.

Both are set in the user modal — see Managing Users.

The folder tree in the user modal. Checking a folder grants it and everything inside it.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• New non-owner accounts are granted nothing. Default-deny, deliberately. A brand-new Reader sees an empty library until you grant something.
  • A granted library with no folders checked shows nothing. The library grant alone is not access — it only makes the library eligible.
  • A folder grant covers that folder and all of its descendants. Nested inheritance is automatic; you never have to check children individually. Checking the library root grants the whole library.
  • Ancestor folders are traversable, but not readable. If you grant /data/Comics/Marvel/Daredevil, the user can walk down through /data/Comics and /data/Comics/Marvel to reach it. Siblings they weren't granted stay hidden, and an ancestor alone never allows opening a file.
  • Store Owners bypass all of it and always see everything.

docs.title: Scenario → what the user sees
docs.text: Scenario What the user sees Library not granted The library does not appear at all. Direct paths into it return 403. Library granted, no folders checked The library appears but is empty. Nothing inside it can be opened. A subfolder granted That folder and everything beneath it, in full — browse, covers, reader, download. An ancestor of a grant The ancestor is navigable so the user can reach the grant below it. Ungranted siblings inside it are hidden, and files sitting directly in the ancestor cannot be opened. Library root granted The entire library. Store Owner Everything, regardless of grants.

docs.title: Enforcement is not just a UI filter
docs.text:
Two independent mechanisms are in play, and both are active:

  1. Listing filtering — anything the user isn't granted never appears in a response.
  2. Path guarding — a hand-typed path into an ungranted area is rejected with 403, even though nothing in the UI offered it.

Path guarding covers browse, search, recent files, thumbnails, covers, the reader, downloads, the metadata browser, OPDS, and /api/v1. A Reader or Clerk API token is scoped to its user's grants, so it cannot reach files the person behind it cannot reach in the browser.

Recently Added respects grants too

Dashboard surfaces that pull from across the library — Recently Added in particular — are filtered to the folders the user has been granted, so nobody stumbles onto something you have not shared with them.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
You have one library at /data/Comics, containing Marvel, DC, and Mature.

To give a Reader everything except Mature:

  1. Grant them the /data/Comics library.
  2. In folder access, check Marvel and DC — but not Mature, and not the library root.

They now see Marvel and DC in full. Mature is invisible in listings, and typing its path returns 403.

docs.title: Managing Users
docs.text:
Accounts are managed from the Users tab in Settings, reached from the gear menu. The tab is Store Owner only — Readers and Clerks cannot see it, and cannot reach it by URL.

Settings → Users, listing every account with its role and status.

docs.title: Adding or editing a user
docs.text:
Everything about an account lives in one modal, so you can create a user and grant their access in a single pass.

Field Description Username The login name. Must be unique. Display Name What the app shows in the header and on shared surfaces. Optional — falls back to the username. Password Set on creation, and changed here later. Stored werkzeug-hashed, never in plaintext. Leave blank when editing to keep the current password. Role Reader, Clerk, or Store Owner. Determines what the account can do. Active Unchecking this blocks login without deleting the account or its reading data. Library access Which libraries this account can see at all. New non-owner accounts get none by default. Folder access Which folders within each granted library the account can see. A granted library with no folders checked shows nothing. API tokens Mint or revoke API tokens for this account. Users can also do this themselves from My Account.

Grants and roles are independent

Role decides what an account can do; grants decide which files it can do it to. A Clerk with no library grants can open the File Manager and see nothing in it.

docs.title: Deactivating vs. deleting
docs.text:
Action What happens Use it when Deactivate (uncheck Active) The account can no longer log in. Its reading history, positions, favorites, reading lists, and stats are all kept. Existing API tokens stop resolving. Someone is leaving temporarily, or you want to suspend access without losing their data. Delete The account and its personal data are removed. The account is genuinely finished with.

Deactivation is reversible; deletion is not. When in doubt, deactivate.

docs.title: Last Store Owner protection
docs.text:
You cannot lock yourself out

CLU refuses to demote, deactivate, or delete the last active Store Owner — the API returns cannot remove the last Store Owner (or cannot delete the last Store Owner) and the change is rejected.

If you want to hand the store over, promote the new owner first, then demote or delete the old one.

There is no in-app recovery for a forgotten owner password, so this protection is the only thing standing between you and a locked app. See First Run & Logging In.

docs.title: My Account
docs.text:
New in v6.3

Appearance and Dashboard Layout are new in v6.3. The API Tokens pane arrived in v6.2.

My Account (/account) is where every user — Reader included — manages the things that belong to them alone. It has three panes.

Pane What it controls Who can change it Appearance Your Bootswatch theme. Every user, for themselves. Dashboard Layout The order of the homepage sections, and which are hidden. Every user, for themselves. API Tokens Your own tokens for /api/v1 and the mobile/desktop clients. Every user, for themselves. A Store Owner can also mint and revoke tokens for any account from Settings → Users.

docs.title: Getting there
docs.text:
Once there's a session, the top navigation gains a person-icon dropdown with My Account, API Tokens, and Logout.

Single-user installs look exactly the same

The person-icon dropdown only appears when there's a session, so an install running in implicit-owner mode is visually unchanged. You still reach My Account from the gear menu.

docs.title: How your settings resolve
docs.text:
Each personal setting resolves in three steps, stopping at the first one that exists:

  1. Your personal override — what you set here.
  2. The owner's site default — what the Store Owner set in Personalization.
  3. The hardcoded default — CLU's built-in fallback.

A user with no override follows the site default. That is not a copy of it — it tracks it, so when the owner changes the site default your view changes with it.

Each pane shows a badge telling you which state you're in:

Badge Meaning Following site default You have no override. The owner's default applies now and will keep applying if they change it. Custom You have set a personal override. The owner's default no longer affects you.

The Reset button on a pane deletes your override and returns you to Following site default.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
The Appearance pane, showing the theme picker with a Custom badge and a Reset button.

Pick any of CLU's Bootswatch themes. The change is yours alone — a Reader choosing a dark theme does not alter what the owner or anyone else sees.

Note

The Default theme and the Zephyr theme are the only officially supported themes. The rest are provided as-is.

docs.title: Dashboard Layout
docs.text:
The Dashboard Layout pane. Reorder sections and hide the ones you don't use.

Reorder the homepage sections and hide any you don't want. Hiding Discover now hides it for you, not for everybody.

For an explanation of each section, see the Collection page.

docs.title: API Tokens
docs.text:
There are two ways an account gets a token:

  • Self-service — you mint your own here. A token only ever authenticates as its owner, so it grants no privilege you don't already have.
  • Owner-minted — a Store Owner mints one for any account from the user modal in Settings → Users.

Shown once

Tokens are stored hashed. The plaintext value is displayed exactly once, when it's created. Copy it immediately — if you lose it, you must revoke the token and mint a new one.

docs.title: What a token can reach
docs.text:
• /api/v1 resolves the bearer token to its user, so reading progress, favorites, and library scope all land on the right account. Reader and Clerk tokens are library-scoped — a token cannot reach files outside its user's grants.
  • The legacy global token still works and maps to the Store Owner, so existing clients keep running untouched.
  • /api/insights accepts the same tokens as an optional Authorization: Bearer <token> header. With a token, the reading counters reflect that user; without one they reflect the Store Owner, so existing tokenless widgets are unchanged. An unknown or malformed token returns 401.

docs.title: OPDS
docs.text: OPDS readers authenticate with HTTP Basic Auth using the account's own username and password — not a token. /opds/browse and /opds/to-read filter to the authenticated user, and bad credentials return 401. In implicit-owner mode OPDS stays auth-free exactly as before.

docs.title: Revoking a token
docs.text: Revoking takes effect immediately. Any client still using that token starts getting 401 on its next call, so re-authenticate the client with a fresh token before you revoke the old one if you want no interruption.

docs.title: No migration on upgrade
docs.text:
No migration

Upgrading changes nothing. Every account starts out with no overrides, which means every account follows the site default — exactly the behavior you had before per-user settings existed. Nobody's view changes until they choose to change it.

docs.title: Per-User Data
docs.text: Sharing a library shouldn't mean sharing a reading history. Nearly everything personal in CLU is scoped to the account that created it.

docs.title: What is yours alone
docs.text: Data Notes Read history and read/unread state Marking an issue read never changes what anyone else sees. Reading positions Where you left off in an issue. These follow a file through renames, moves, and CBR→CBZ conversion. To Read / Want to Read Including bookmarked reading lists. On the Stack Built from your own subscriptions and your own bookmarked lists. Favorite series and favorite publishers Reading lists Insights, the reading timeline, and CLU Wrapped Backed by a per-user stats cache, so one user's numbers can never be served to another. Recently Added Also filtered to the folders you've been granted. Theme Your own Bootswatch theme. (New in v6.3.) Dashboard layout Your own section order and hidden sections. (New in v6.3.) API tokens See My Account.

docs.title: Operations and notifications
docs.text: Long-running operations and their toast notifications are scoped to whoever triggered them. The progress indicator shows your jobs, not everybody's. The Store Owner still sees the whole picture.

docs.title: Still shared
docs.text:
Still shared

Two things remain app-wide rather than per user:

  • Komga sync targets a single shared server and account, attributed to the Store Owner. Every user's sync activity lands on that one connection. This is a known follow-up.
  • The AI recommendation service is configured once, globally. It is not a display preference — the toggle gates an owner-configured service holding a shared API key, so exposing it per user would mean handing every account the ability to spend against the owner's key.

Everything else that used to be app-wide — notably the theme and the dashboard layout — is now per user. See My Account.

docs.title: Roles & Permissions
docs.text: CLU has three roles in a strict hierarchy — reader < clerk < owner — and each role inherits everything below it. A Clerk can do everything a Reader can; a Store Owner can do everything a Clerk can.

docs.title: What each role can do
docs.text:
Role Can do Reader Browse and read comics, track their own reading history and reading position, keep their own favorites, To Read list, and stats, view reading lists, set their own theme and dashboard layout, and manage their own API tokens. Clerk Everything a Reader can do, plus file management, renaming, metadata and scraping, downloads, the Pull List, Wanted Issues, Weekly Packs, and Releases. Store Owner Everything a Clerk can do, plus app settings, user management, library and folder grants, provider credentials, database tools, Problem Files, logs, and system actions.

Clerk role maturity

The Clerk role is active but less widely tested than Reader and Store Owner. If something in the Clerk surface behaves unexpectedly, please report it.

docs.title: Minimum role by feature
docs.text: Feature / page Minimum role Collection browsing and the reader Reader Reading Lists — viewing and bookmarking Reader Reading Lists — Track Wanted (new in v6.5) Clerk My Account — theme, dashboard layout, own API tokens Reader File Manager and all file operations Clerk Pull List, Releases, Wanted, Weekly Packs, Series Search, Publishers Clerk Download Status and grabbing from any source Clerk Metadata scraping, Metadata History, Source Wall Clerk App Logs Clerk Settings — every tab Store Owner Users — creating accounts, roles, library and folder grants Store Owner Library and publisher create/edit/delete, provider credentials Store Owner Database tools, Database Recovery, Schedules, GCD import, restart, rebuild index Store Owner Problem Files and Find a replacement Store Owner

docs.title: The default policy
docs.text:
Anything not explicitly classified falls back to a simple rule:

  • Reads (GET) default to Reader.
  • Mutations (POST / PUT / DELETE / PATCH) default to Clerk.
  • Store Owners always pass.

The default is deliberately conservative: a new endpoint that nobody has classified is Clerk-gated rather than open.

docs.title: Readers may still POST their own personal data
docs.text:
The mutation-means-Clerk default has a carve-out for data that belongs to the person making the request. Readers can write:

  • Read history and read/unread state
  • Reading position (where they left off in an issue)
  • Reading stats
  • Favorites
  • To Read and On the Stack
  • Their own theme and dashboard layout
  • Their own API tokens

Everything in that list is scoped to the requesting user, so a Reader can never write over somebody else's copy. See Per-User Data.

Why Bookmark is Reader but Track Wanted is not

Both buttons sit next to each other on a reading list, so the split is worth stating.

Bookmarking a list is personal data — it changes one person's dashboard and nothing else. Track Wanted spends bandwidth and disk: every unmatched entry in the list becomes a wanted issue that the nightly sweep searches for and downloads. That's a shared consequence, so it takes the role that manages the list.

Gating is not just cosmetic

Role enforcement covers both nav visibility and direct-URL access. Hiding a menu item is a convenience; typing the URL for a page above your role returns 403, and so does calling its API directly.

docs.title: Guided Setup
docs.text:
Guided Setup helps you go from a clean install to a working library in a few minutes.

It checks your default settings, asks what you want to do with CLU, and then shows only the settings based on what you need.

On an existing install, it works as a health check: what is configured, what is broken, and highlights what's not being used.

Guided Setup doesn't replace Settings. A change in one, shows up in the other. Each step also links to the matching Settings tab for the options the walkthrough doesn't cover.

docs.title: When it opens
docs.text:
Install What happens New install The Store Owner's (Admin) first visit to the home page opens Guided Setup. This happens once: after that, the home page opens normally. Upgraded install Nothing is redirected. Instead, the Store Owner (Admin) sees a one-time banner: "New: Guided Setup can check your configuration and point out anything missing." with Run Guided Setup and Dismiss. Opening Guided Setup or dismissing the banner removes it for good.

Users are never redirected and never see the banner.

docs.title: Running it again
docs.text:
You can re-run Guided Setup at any time from either of these:

  • The Run Guided Setup button above the tabs on the Settings page.
  • gear menu → Guided Setup, between Settings and Schedules.

docs.title: Step 1: System Check
docs.text:
The first step is a read-only check of the install. Each row is an OK, a warning or a failure, or is skipped when it can't run on your platform. A row that isn't OK shows how to fix it and links to more details.

Only the Database check blocks you. If it fails, Next stays disabled until it's fixed. Everything else is a warning you can come back to. Run again repeats the check after you've changed something.

Check What it means How to fix a warning Database CLU can open its database, and no corruption has been reported. If it can't be opened, check that /config is mounted and writable, then restart the container. The container log shows the underlying error. If corruption was reported, open Settings → Database to run a full check and repair or restore it. See Database. Database storage The filesystem holding /config is safe for a database. A network share (CIFS/NFS) or the container's own temporary layer is not. Mount /config on local storage or a Docker named volume. See Volumes and permissions. /config is writable/cache is writable CLU can create and delete a file in each. /config holds the database, its backups and the logs; /cache holds thumbnails and the trash. Map a volume onto that path that the container user (PUID:PGID) can write to. Comic folders under /data A comics volume is mapped. CLU lists the folders it finds under /data; the Libraries step uses that list. Map your comics folder into the container under /data in docker-compose.yaml (for example /mnt/comics:/data/comics), then recreate the container. An empty /data is fine if your libraries are mapped somewhere else, such as /comics. WATCH folderTARGET folder The Folder Monitoring folders are outside /data and writable. Unset, they default to /downloads/temp and /downloads/processed. Set them in Settings → File Processing to folders mapped into the container outside /data. The container user must be able to write to them. Libraries Shown only when no library exists yet. Add one in the next steps, or in Settings → Libraries. Library: name One row per enabled library: the path exists, is a folder, and can be read and written. A missing path usually means the volume mapping changed: check docker-compose.yaml, or edit the library's path. A read-only library still works, but renaming, metadata writes and conversion will fail. Give the container user write access, or set PUID/PGID to the folder's owner. Owner account The owner account exists and, if login is required, has a password. A single-user, login-free install is OK as it is. If login is required and the owner has no password, set one in the Users step or on the Users page. Container user CLU runs as your PUID, not as root, and your library folders are owned by the same user. Make the mounted folders writable by PUID:PGID (fix the volume's ownership, or set PUID/PGID to match it) and recreate the container.

Info

Every check gives up after 5 seconds, so one hung mount can't stall the page. That warning almost always means a network mount (CIFS/NFS) has stopped responding. Check the share on the host, then Run again.

docs.title: Volumes and permissions
docs.text:
Most warnings come down to the volume mapping in your docker-compose.yaml. Guided Setup can't change it, because it runs inside the container, but it can tell you what's wrong:

  • Paths are container paths. CLU only sees what you map. A folder on your NAS has to be mapped to a path under /data (or another mapped volume) before you can add it as a library.
  • PUID/PGID must match the owner of your folders. When a mount isn't writable by PUID:PGID, the container falls back to running as root, and every file it writes is then root-owned.
  • Recreate, don't just restart. A changed volume or environment variable needs docker compose up -d, not just a restart.

See Config Installation and the Quickstart for the full docker-compose.yaml.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: The System Check runs a quick check that the database opens, and reports any corruption CLU has already recorded. Settings → Database runs the full integrity check, and is where you repair or restore. See Database and Database Recovery.

docs.title: Step 2: How do you plan to use CLU?
docs.text:
Your answers decide which steps come next. You can change them by coming back to this step.

Do you already have comics organized in folders?

  • No, I'm starting fresh: you go through every section in order, and each one can be skipped. The two sections that need an existing collection, Mylar3 Import and Pull List Scan, are left out.
  • Yes: pick any of the use cases below. You get each section the use cases need, once, however many of them ask for it.
Use case What it's for Sections it adds Repair and fix my existing collection Rename, convert CBR to CBZ, and find damaged or duplicate files. Libraries, Folder Monitoring, Notifications, Library Health Add or update metadata Tag comics with ComicInfo.xml from Metron, ComicVine or GCD. Libraries, Metadata Import from Mylar3 Bring over your watchlist, download client, indexers and ComicVine key. Libraries, Metadata, Mylar3 Import, Downloads Map existing folders to my pull list Read series.json/cvinfo in your folders to build the Pull List. Libraries, Metadata, Pull List Scan Subscribe and download comics Follow series and download new issues automatically. Libraries, Metadata, Folder Monitoring, Downloads, Schedules, Users, Notifications Read my comics and track stats Nothing extra is needed beyond a library. Libraries, Users

Personalization is part of every path.

Metron is required for three of these

Importing from Mylar3, mapping folders to the Pull List, and subscribing to series all need a Metron account. The Pull List, Wanted and subscriptions are built on Metron's release data. ComicVine is optional.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
Sections always run in this order, and each one appears only if your indicated usage includes it:

Libraries → Metadata → Mylar3 Import → Pull List Scan → Folder Monitoring → Downloads → Schedules → Users → Notifications → Personalization → Library Health → Summary

The Set Up CLU tab of this documentation follows the same order, and the Library Health's pages are under Maintenance.

Every step has the same basic layout:

  • Definition of the section
  • Important Fields
  • Save (and Test where it applies)
  • Link to the full Settings tab
  • Link to the docs

Each step saves as you go, so there's no "save everything" at the end.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
A library is a folder CLU indexes and shows in the collection. The step lists the folders the System Check found under /data, each with a one-click Add as library, and has a folder picker for anywhere else you've mapped.

Generally you would add your root folder and CLU will traverse the directories.

Adding a library starts the file index, and the step shows its progress.

More in Libraries.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Set up the the CLU supported metadata providers. Metron is required for the Pull List; ComicVine and GCD are optional - but recommended. You can test credentials before you save them. This step can also download the ComicVine local database for you, and sets the ComicInfo.xml write options.

More in Metadata Providers and Local Metadata Databases.

docs.title: Mylar3 Import
docs.text: Checks that you have a library and Metron set up, then opens the Mylar3 importer. The importer's Back to Guided Setup button returns you to this step, which shows the result of your last import. You must upload your existing mylar.db file and config.ini.

docs.title: Pull List Scan
docs.text: Runs Scan Library from inside the walkthrough. It reads the series.json and cvinfo files in your folders and maps each series to the Pull List. Folders that need a decision open in the Pull List page's review window, where you confirm them. This is less accurate than the Mylar3 import, but if you don't have the database and config files, it's a good place to start.

docs.title: Folder Monitoring
docs.text:
Sets the WATCH and TARGET folders with the folder picker, then turns monitoring on. Here too: auto-convert, auto-rename with a live preview of your rename pattern, and the trash.

WATCH is where you drop files and folders to be processed. Files are also downloaded here from DDL, Usenet and DC++. This should be outside of your library. All files dropped here will have filenames cleaned and will be coverted to CBZ files. They are then moved to the TARGET folder.

TARGET is where CLU moves processed files. This is a TEMP directory that holds all files until they are matched & moved via the automated process or you manually move them via File Manager

More in Monitoring Setup and File Processing Settings.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
Choose which sources CLU downloads from: DDL (Direct Downloads), Usenet and DC++. A source is used only while it's ticked, and the ticked ones are tried in the order shown. You can reorder them and enable/disable as needed.

  • DDL works out of the box and requires no configuration. Adding a PixelDrain API key is optional and allows faster downloads of large files.
  • Usenet needs a SABnzbd or NZBGet client and at least one Newznab indexer.
  • DC++ needs an AirDC++ client.

For clients and indexers, Save is enabled only after a passing Test of what's on screen.

More in Download & API Settings, Adding a Download Client, Adding Newznab Indexers, Adding AirDC++ and Source Priority.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
Pick your timezone and set the recurring jobs: the file index rebuild, series sync, GetComics auto-download and reading-list sync. Use recommended defaults turns the rebuild and sync on daily at off-peak times. Times are shown in your timezone.

More in Schedules.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Will anyone else use this CLU?

  • No: CLU stays login-free. That's fine for one person on a private network.
  • Yes: set the owner's username and password, then optionally add a second account. Adding that account is what turns login on.

More in Users & Access.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Add Apprise URLs and choose which events notify you. Test works before you save.

See the Appriseit.com Services list for the URL format of each service. Lines starting with # are ignored.

More in Notifications.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text:
Pick the site theme, with previews.

More in Personalization.

docs.title: Library Health
docs.text:
Turn on the library health scan, set how often it runs, and run one now. The step then shows what the scan found, with links to where you fix things:

  • Problem Files: damaged archives, failed conversions, orphans and empty folders.
  • Duplicates: exact and likely duplicate copies.
  • Source Wall: edit ComicInfo.xml across a folder, and see which provider tagged each file.

docs.title: Skipping and resuming
docs.text:
Button What it does Skip this step Marks the step Skipped and moves on. You can come back to it from the progress rail or the Summary. Skip setup Leaves Guided Setup and goes to the home page. You won't be redirected again; run it from Settings or the gear menu when you want. All Settings Opens the full Settings page.

Your place is saved on every Next and Skip. If you leave midway, reopening Guided Setup picks up at the step you were on.

docs.title: The Summary
docs.text:
The last step shows one row per section:

Status Meaning Configured The section is set up and working. Needs attention Something is set up but broken, or incomplete. The row says what. Not set up Nothing is configured yet. Skipped You skipped the step and it still isn't configured. Configure in Settings The section has no step in the walkthrough.

Each row has Open step, which takes you back to it (adding it to your path if it wasn't there), and Settings or Open page for the full options. Under the table, the System Check runs again.

  • Finish marks Guided Setup complete and goes to the home page.
  • Download summary (for support) saves clu-setup-summary.json: your path, skipped steps, section statuses and the System Check results. Attach it when you ask for help on Discord or GitHub.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Docker Hub images are available for quick installation and deploy.

New to Docker on Windows?

Installing CLU on Windows with Docker Desktop walks through every step, from installing Docker Desktop to opening CLU in your browser.

docs.title: Install via Docker Compose
docs.text:
services:
    comic-utils:
        image: allaboutduncan/comic-utils-web:latest

        container_name: clu
        logging:
            driver: "json-file"
            options:
                max-size: '20m'  # Reduce log size to 20MB
                max-file: '3'     # Keep only 3 rotated files
        restart: always
        ports:
            - '5577:5577'
        volumes:
            ## REQUIRED. Without this, the database lives in the container's own
            ## writable layer and is destroyed on the next image update.
            - 'config-volume:/config' # Maps to a Docker Volume for Database Storage and Backups
            - "/path/to/local/cache:/cache" # Maps to local folder for thumbnail cache
            ## update the line below to map to your library.
            ## Map your first/main library to /data
            - "/e/Comics:/data"
            ## Map additional drives/libraries and add them in the app settings
            - "/f/Magazines:/magazines"
            ## Additional folder if you want to use Folder Monitoring.
            - "/f/Downloads:/downloads"
        environment:
            - FLASK_ENV=production
            ## Set the User ID (PUID) and Group ID (PGID) for the container.
            ## This is often needed to resolve permission issues, especially on systems like Unraid
            ## where a specific user/group owns the files.
            ## For Unraid, PUID is typically 99 (user 'nobody') and PGID is typically 100 (group 'users').
            ## For Windows/WSL, you need to set these to match your Windows user ID (see WINDOWS_WSL_SETUP.md)
            - PUID=99
            - PGID=100
            ## File creation mask. 000 -> world-writable folders (drwxrwsrwx) and files
            ## (-rw-rw-rw-). Use 002 for group-writable (775/664) or 022 for owner-only writes.
            - UMASK=000
volumes:
  config-volume: # Required for Database Storage and Backups

docs.title: Install via Docker
docs.text:
docker run -d \
  --name clu \
  --restart always \
  -p 5577:5577 \
  --log-driver json-file \
  --log-opt max-size=20m \
  --log-opt max-file=3 \
  -v config-volume:/config \
  -v /path/to/local/cache:/cache \
  -v /e/Comics:/data \
  -v /f/Magazines:/magazines \
  -v /f/Downloads:/downloads \
  -e FLASK_ENV=production \
  -e PUID=99 \
  -e PGID=100 \
  -e UMASK=000 \
  allaboutduncan/comic-utils-web:latest

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Additional info about the ENV variables can be found here.

Parameter Function -p 5577:5577 The port exposed by the app for the web interface. - 'config-volume:/config' Maps to a Docker Volume for Database Storage and Backups -v /User/comics:/data Location of your library to manage. Must be mapped to /data -v /User/downloads:/downloads Optional folder to configure for Folder Monitoring. -e FLASK_ENV=development Set to 'development' for local development. -e PUID=99 Set the User ID (PUID) for the container. -e PGID=100 Set the Group ID (PGID) for the container. -e UMASK=000 Set the file creation mask (UMASK).

Accounts and logins

CLU is login-free with a single account. Real user accounts, roles, and per-folder permissions are covered in Users & Access.

docs.title: Next: Guided Setup
docs.text: Once CLU is running, open it in your browser. On a new install, Guided Setup opens on your first visit: it checks your volumes and permissions, then walks you through libraries, metadata and the rest.
